summary: Amazon's stock underperformed in 2021, rising only 2.4%, far below its Big Tech peers. The company's retail division struggled, with revenue growth slowing to 27% in Q2 2021, down from 41% in the same period the previous year. This decline was attributed to a return to pre-pandemic spending habits as more Americans got vaccinated. Rising costs in retail, including coronavirus-related expenses like safety measures and physical network expansion, and global supply chain constraints led to billions in extra costs during Q4 2021. Amazon raised wages and offered bonuses to attract workers and reroute packages to adequately staffed facilities. These factors negatively impacted its stock performance in 2021. Analysts noted that Amazon faced easier year-over-year comparisons in 2022 after growth moderated in 2021. Some pandemic-related investments in supply chain and logistics may start to yield benefits, but challenges like inflationary pressures, supply chain constraints, and labor issues could still affect its stock. Despite this, several analysts have named Amazon as a top pick for 2022, citing expectations for a rebound in its e-commerce business.

The U.S. Department of the Treasury introduced a new methodology for estimating holdings of Treasury securities, effective with the February 29, 2012 release. This update incorporates new data from the TIC Form SLT, which reports long-term Treasury securities held by foreign investors. The SLT data, collected in September and December 2011, includes holdings of long-term securities (original maturity of more than one year), such as Treasury securities. Short-term Treasury holdings are reported on TIC Form BL-2, which includes data on short-term liabilities to foreigners. Starting in January 2012, SLT data will be collected monthly, with the MFH table updated on a rolling basis. The new methodology also integrates net transactions data to estimate holdings for the most recent month. Revised data for October and November 2011 reflect this new approach, combining SLT data with net purchases. Data for earlier months through August 2011 are based on the previous methodology. Periodic surveys, conducted annually since June 2002, provide the starting position for long-term Treasury holdings, with the most recent survey as of June 2011. Estimates between surveys are constructed by adding monthly net purchases to the latest survey data. The U.S. Department of the Treasury provides estimates of holdings of Treasury securities, which are influenced by custodial and transaction biases. For example, a German investor holding U.S. securities through a Swiss bank is recorded under Switzerland rather than Germany, contributing to the large recorded holdings in major custodial centers like Switzerland and Luxembourg. The methodology for estimating holdings has evolved to reduce distortions caused by transaction bias, which previously led to significant geographic discrepancies. The new methodology relies on transactions data for the most recent month, minimizing the impact of transaction bias over time. Holdings of short-term Treasury bills are reported at face value, while long-term securities are reported at market value. Data on short-term holdings is collected through the TIC form BL-2, and long-term holdings are estimated using periodic surveys and monthly net purchase data. The latest survey data for long-term holdings is as of June 2005, with earlier data available for previous years.

summary: A new Care.com survey indicates that the lack of school and child care options is pushing some parents out of the workforce. Over 73% of parents with children under 15 plan to make major changes to their professional lives due to the lack of child care. About 15% are considering leaving the workforce altogether. Deb Perelman, founder of Smitten Kitchen, warns that working parents may face "compassion fatigue" from workplaces as they continue to balance work and child care responsibilities. Nearly 66% of respondents reported that their productivity at work has suffered, and over 55% feel they are letting down their colleagues. About 65% of working parents start late or end their workday early to care for their children. The struggle to balance work and child care has impacted their ability to perform well at work, with 64% reporting at least one major work failure since the pandemic began. Only 15% of working parents receive employer-sponsored child-care benefits, highlighting the need for more support and resources. A June report from the University of Oregon's RAPID-EC Research Group also highlights the lack of child care and school options is pushing some parents out of the workforce. Nearly half, 47% of working families, have lost the child care they used before the pandemic. Of families using child-care centers, 60% reported losing their provider. Congress allocated $3.5 billion in emergency funding to child care in the CARES Act, helping 23 states offer grants to child-care providers. However, more than 40% of child-care centers remain closed in some states, and most report the funds are already gone. The House of Representatives passed a set of bills last week that would provide over $60 billion in direct funding to the child-care industry. Democrats are pushing to get these provisions included in the next comprehensive relief package, but the Republican-led legislation has only allocated $15 billion toward child care and $70 billion for K-12 schools. Experts say it will likely take actions by both the government and employers to ensure that there's no lasting effects on working parents as they continue to juggle work and child-care responsibilities. Parents are faced with tough decisions for the upcoming school year, as many operate without child-care benefits. Kate Delany, a New Jersey-based mother, is struggling to balance her work responsibilities with managing homeschooling for her 8- and 11-year-old kids. Her husband, a middle school teacher, is planning to go back full-time this fall, adding to the stress. Delany says she is unsure what the fall will look like for her family, as her kids want to go back to school, but she prefers remote learning.

summary: On March 3, 2016, the Federal Reserve Board (FRB) released a FEDS Note titled 'Funding Agreement-Backed Securities in the Financial Accounts of the United States.' This note outlines a new method for accounting for funding agreement-backed securities (FABS), which are securities created by special purpose entities (SPEs) that securitize funding agreements. These agreements are deposit-type contracts sold by life insurance companies, allowing funds to accumulate at a guaranteed rate of return over a specified period. The note highlights risks such as liquidity and maturity transformation, which can impact financial stability. Data on FABS issuance began in 1997:Q3, with foreign FABS outstanding peaking at $48 billion in 2004:Q3 and declining to $5 billion by 2015:Q3. Domestic FABS peaked at $140 billion in 2008:Q2 and contracted sharply during the global financial crisis. The new data allows for better categorization of funding agreements, distinguishing those backing FABS from pension entitlements. The FRB also updated the Financial Accounts to include funding agreements in the asset-backed securities (ABS) sector, increasing both financial assets and liabilities by the same amount. This change affects the life insurance sector table (L.116), where funding agreements are now categorized separately as 'funding agreements backing securities' for domestic SPEs, while foreign SPEs' purchases are included as part of foreign direct investment in the U.S.

President-elect Donald Trump's proposed tariffs on Mexican cars may not stop the trend of U.S. automakers moving production to Mexico. Despite Trump's criticism of General Motors for building the Chevrolet Cruze in Mexico, Ford announced it would scrap plans to build a $1.6 billion plant there. U.S. automakers Ford, GM, and Fiat Chrysler are still planning to manufacture nearly 1 million more cars in Mexico by 2022, while producing half a million fewer in the U.S. Mexico's appeal lies in its trade agreements with 44 countries, giving automakers access to half the global car market tariff-free, compared to the U.S.'s 20 countries. Mexican workers are paid significantly less, with total hourly compensation in the motor vehicle manufacturing sector being about 80% less than in the U.S. This cost advantage, combined with trade agreements, makes Mexico an attractive location for automakers, even as Trump pushes for more protectionist policies. Automakers can save significant costs by producing vehicles in Mexico due to lower labor costs and favorable trade agreements. For a typical midsize car, an automaker can save $600 per vehicle on labor costs. However, additional shipping expenses to the U.S. and Europe add to the costs, making the overall savings from Mexico still substantial. Automakers save $1,500 per car on cheaper Mexican auto parts and that the U.S. lacks as many free trade agreements as Mexico, leading to higher costs for some parts if produced in the U.S. The cost advantages from Mexico’s trade agreements are significant, with automakers avoiding about $770 million in tariffs in 2014. Mexico sends 2 million cars a year to the U.S., more than half its total production, but by 2018, 28 percent of Mexico’s production will be exported to countries besides the U.S. and Canada. GM and Audi are examples of companies leveraging Mexico’s trade agreements to expand their markets.

summary: Texas has claimed the top spot in CNBC's 2018 America’s Top States for Business rankings, marking its fourth consecutive win in the annual study. The state's energy sector, particularly the rising prices of West Texas Intermediate Crude Oil, has played a significant role in boosting the $1.6 trillion Texas economy. Over the past year, Texas has added more than 350,000 jobs, with the energy sector contributing the largest increase. This growth has also led to a rise in the state's GDP, which increased by 5.2 percent in the fourth quarter of 2017. Texas is home to major companies such as AT&T, ExxonMobil, and Dell, and it ranks highly in several categories, including Infrastructure (No. 1) and Access to Capital (No. 3). The state's economic strength is further supported by its robust workforce and strong business environment. Texas was ranked as America's top state for business in 2018, largely due to its business-friendly regulations, low taxes, and strong energy sector. Governor Greg Abbott emphasized the importance of minimizing taxes, stating, 'The only good tax is a dead tax.' However, Texas faced challenges in areas such as education, where it ranked No. 37, and quality of life, with a high violent crime rate and a significant portion of the population lacking health insurance. The state also scored poorly on inclusiveness, lacking public-accommodation laws to protect against discrimination. Despite these issues, Texas' booming economy, particularly in energy, helped maintain its top position. However, potential budget challenges and external economic factors could threaten its status. Other states like Washington also made strong runs for the top spot, though they faced their own economic and structural challenges.

title: Activities of U.S. Affiliates of Foreign Multinational Enterprises in 2012
summary: The U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) released preliminary statistics on U.S. affiliates of foreign multinational enterprises (MNEs) in 2012. These statistics, based on the 2012 Benchmark Survey of Foreign Direct Investment in the United States, cover financial and operational details of U.S. affiliates, including balance sheet, income statement, employment, employee compensation, capital expenditures, trade in goods, and research and development spending. The data focuses on majority-owned U.S. affiliates. The current-dollar value added of majority-owned U.S. affiliates totaled $773.8 billion in 2012, a 3.7 percent increase from the previous year. However, the growth rate was slower than the value added of all U.S. private industry, leading to a decrease in affiliates’ share of U.S. private industry value added from 6.2 percent in 2011 to 6.1 percent in 2012. U.S. affiliates employed 5.8 million workers in 2012, an increase of 1.3 percent. Exports of goods by affiliates rose 5 percent, while imports of goods by affiliates rose 4 percent. About 60 percent of the goods imported by affiliates were intended for resale without further processing. Research and development (R&D) performed by affiliates rose 6 percent.

summary: Oil prices dipped below $49 as the sector faced a 'Hunger Games' scenario, with analysts warning of a potential sector-wide recession. U.S. crude and Brent futures fell to 5½-year lows, driven by weak global demand and increased U.S. oil production. OPEC's reluctance to cut output further exacerbated the price drop. Bernstein Research likened the situation to the movie 'The Hunger Games,' predicting a structural recession in offshore activity. Moody's warned that E&P companies could cut capital spending by 20% if oil prices average $75 a barrel in 2015, with potential cuts reaching 40% if prices fall below $60. Oilfield services companies could face earnings declines of 12-17% at $75 a barrel and 25-30% at $60. Midstream operators would also face significant earnings pressure. Major oil companies like Shell, BP, ExxonMobil, and Total were expected to be more resilient, while smaller OFS companies like Basic Energy Services and Key Energy Services would face stress. Oil prices dipped below $49 as the energy sector faced significant challenges, with several companies experiencing sharp declines in stock prices. Saipem and Subsea 7 were downgraded to a 'sell' rating, with their stock prices falling by 44% and 34% respectively last year. Norway's Aker Solutions was also downgraded to 'underperform' by Bernstein, while France's Technip remained a key defensive play despite a 30% drop in its stock price. These developments highlight the volatility and uncertainty within the energy sector during this period.

title: US Prosecutors Ask to Pause SEC Action Against Alleged Crypto Scammer
summary: U.S. prosecutors have requested a temporary pause in SEC actions against alleged crypto scammers Manor and Pardo. The request follows a grand jury indictment for wire fraud and securities fraud prior to the SEC complaint. Civil and criminal charges were filed on January 17, with prosecutors arguing that proceeding with the SEC case would allow the defendants to delay and weaken the criminal process. Pardo pleaded not guilty on January 22, while Manor remains at large. The case overlaps with a criminal investigation into the fraudulent BCT token offering, which raised $30 million for digital securities hedge fund technology in 2017-2018. Manor, who was convicted of breach of trust in 2011 related to the Portus hedge fund, later moved to the U.S. to launch Blockchain Terminal. The Block's 2018 investigation revealed that "Shaun MacDonald" leading Blockchain Terminal was actually Manor in disguise. The 275 U.S. investors in the BCT ICO were unaware of Manor's criminal past.

Subaru of America, Inc. has won the Most Trusted Brand category in Kelley Blue Book's 2018 Brand Image Awards for the fourth consecutive year. This recognition highlights Subaru's commitment to delivering safe, reliable, and long-lasting vehicles. The awards are based on new car buyer perception data from the Brand Watch™ study by Kelley Blue Book Strategic Insights. The recognition reflects Subaru's efforts in creating and maintaining brand attributes that resonate with new-vehicle buyers. Subaru of America, Inc. is a wholly owned subsidiary of Subaru Corporation of Japan and operates through a network of over 620 retailers in the United States. The company is guided by the Subaru Love Promise, which emphasizes its commitment to supporting communities and customers. Subaru has donated over $120 million to various causes over the past 20 years and has accumulated over 40,000 volunteer hours from its employees. The company's production facilities are designed with zero-landfill principles, and Subaru of Indiana Automotive, Inc. is the only U.S. automobile plant designated as a backyard wildlife habitat by the National Wildlife Federation. This award underscores Subaru's dedication to customer trust and its role in the automotive industry.

David's Bridal, a wedding dress retailer, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on Monday, November 19, 2018, as part of a restructuring deal with its lenders that will reduce its debt by over $400 million. The company stated that its stores will remain open during the restructuring process, and customers can continue shopping in its more than 300 stores. The bankruptcy is part of a broader strategy to restructure the business, with the company anticipating completion of the court-supervised process by early January. David's Bridal also received commitments for $60 million in new debtor-in-possession financing from existing lenders, along with a recommitment of its existing $125 million asset-backed loan. The bankruptcy reflects broader challenges in the wedding industry, including shifting consumer preferences and the rise of online retailers offering non-traditional wedding attire options. The company acquired digital gift company Blueprint Registry in the summer of 2018 to bolster its online presence, but traditional retailers face difficulties in building the infrastructure needed to support e-commerce expansion. This comes a year after bridal store Alfred Angelo liquidated its business, highlighting the sector's struggles with evolving consumer trends and financial pressures.

The U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) is scheduled to release its annual GDP statistics update on July 30, 2020. This update will include revised GDP estimates for the first quarter of 2020 and the previous five years. The BEA utilizes newly available data and methodological improvements to refine earlier GDP estimates, which are the most comprehensive measure of U.S. economic activity. This year’s update will cover quarterly and annual estimates for 2015 through the first quarter of 2020, with selected updates of income and saving reaching back further. The annual update will be released alongside the first estimate of second quarter GDP at 8:30 a.m. on July 30. The update will incorporate more complete and detailed data from various sources, including the Census Bureau, the federal budget, the IRS, and the Agricultural Department. Additionally, the update will reflect ongoing work to harmonize BEA’s National Income and Product Accounts with its industry statistics. The July update will also include improvements such as the results of the annual update of BEA’s international transactions accounts, updates to seasonal factors, and new subcategories of private fixed investment in intellectual property products. The BEA will also provide downloadable resources, including Acrobat Reader for accessing the detailed reports. The last modification to the page was made on July 13, 2020, indicating the latest update to the release schedule and information.

summary: Intel (INTC) reported its third-quarter earnings on October 21, 2021, revealing a decline in PC chip sales due to industry-wide component shortages. The company attributed the 2% shrinkage in its PC chip business to reduced laptop volumes and a lack of other parts needed for assembling computers. Intel also warned that its gross margin and free cash flow would decline over the next two to three years due to increased capital expenditure, including a $20 billion investment in new chip factories and a semiconductor foundry in Arizona. Despite the challenges, Intel's Data Center Group saw a 10% year-over-year revenue increase to $6.5 billion, driven by demand for on-premise servers. CEO Pat Gelsinger stated that PC demand remains strong, though the semiconductor shortage is expected to persist until 2023. Analysts suggest the pandemic-driven PC surge may be waning, but Gelsinger believes the PC business is now structurally larger, with daily sales reaching a million units. Intel reported a gross margin of 56% for Q3 2021, up 2.9% year-over-year. The company plans to transition into a foundry business, manufacturing chips for other designers, in addition to its own processors. This shift is expected to be costly but could benefit from government support in the U.S. and Europe. Intel also noted growth in its internet of things group, which increased 54% to $1 billion, and Mobileye, its automotive chip subsidiary, which grew 39% to $326 million. Intel's CFO, George Davis, announced his retirement in May 2022. The company will provide more details on its foundry transition and technology roadmap at its analyst day in February 2022.

summary: General Electric (GE) shares rose 7.76% on Tuesday following the announcement of its plan to spin off its health-care unit. The move is part of a broader strategy to refocus GE's operations on aviation, power, and renewable energy businesses. CEO John Flannery stated that the company will maintain its current quarterly dividend until the spinoff is completed and then adjust it in line with industrial peers. Flannery also mentioned that the company is likely to lower its aggregate dividend once the health-care spinoff is finished. GE also plans to reduce its net debt by about $25 billion by 2020 and generate $500 million or more in corporate cost savings by the end of 2020. Moody's Investors Service reaffirmed its A2 rating for GE but maintained a negative outlook for its debt due to expected continued weakness in earnings and cash flows through 2019 and into 2020. The company will also fully separate its stake in Baker Hughes, a GE company (BHGE). GE’s Board of Directors unanimously approved the plan, which includes separating GE Healthcare into a standalone company and pursuing an orderly separation from BHGE over the next two to three years. John Flannery, chairman and CEO of GE, emphasized that the spin-off would create a pure-play healthcare company and a tier-one oil and gas servicing and equipment player. GE also aims to reduce its industrial net debt by approximately $25 billion by 2020 and maintain more than $15 billion of cash on the balance sheet. The new GE Operating System will result in a smaller corporate headquarters focused on strategy, capital allocation, talent, and governance. GE expects to maintain its current quarterly dividend until GE Healthcare is established as an independent entity. Kieran Murphy, president and CEO of GE Healthcare, will continue to lead the unit as a standalone company, maintaining the GE brand.

summary: On July 29, 2014, the U.S. Department of the Treasury announced additional sanctions targeting three Russian state-owned financial institutions and one Russian state-owned defense technology entity. These actions were taken in response to Russia’s continued efforts to destabilize eastern Ukraine. The Treasury imposed prohibitions under Executive Order (E.O.) 13662, limiting U.S. persons from providing new financing to Bank of Moscow, Russian Agricultural Bank, and VTB Bank OAO. These measures also included designating United Shipbuilding Corporation under E.O. 13661 for its involvement in the arms and related materiel sector. The sanctions aim to increase financial pressure on the Russian government and limit its access to U.S. capital markets. The Treasury emphasized that these actions, along with those by the European Union, significantly raise the costs for Russia’s actions in Ukraine. The sanctioned entity, a shipbuilding corporation, designs and constructs ships for the Russian Navy and is the largest shipbuilding company in Russia. This designation expands the list of eight defense technology firms previously targeted on July 16. Under E.O. 13661, any assets of the designated entity within U.S. jurisdiction must be frozen, and transactions involving the entity by U.S. persons or within the United States are generally prohibited.

On February 8, 2012, the U.S. Department of the Treasury and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) issued proposed regulations under the Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act (FATCA) to improve offshore tax compliance and reduce the burden on U.S. taxpayers. These regulations aim to address non-compliance by U.S. taxpayers using foreign accounts. The proposed rules outline a step-by-step process for identifying U.S. accounts, reporting information, and meeting withholding requirements for foreign financial institutions (FFIs), other foreign entities, and U.S. withholding agents. The regulations are implemented in stages to minimize administrative burdens and costs while achieving FATCA’s compliance objectives. The rules also allow time for resolving local law limitations that may affect some FFIs. The Treasury and IRS emphasized that these regulations are targeted and efficient, complementing global efforts to combat offshore tax evasion. The proposed regulations include measures to reduce administrative burdens, expand the categories of FFIs deemed compliant with FATCA, and phase in reporting and withholding obligations over an extended transition period. Additionally, the Treasury Department issued a joint statement with several European governments expressing mutual intent to pursue a government-to-government framework for implementing FATCA.

summary: The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 623.34 points, or 2.4%, to close at 25,628.90 on Friday, following President Donald Trump's directive for U.S. manufacturers to seek alternatives to China. Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell's speech at the Jackson Hole symposium did not provide clarity on potential rate cuts, leaving traders uncertain about the Fed's stance on monetary policy. The Dow plunged after Trump ordered manufacturers to leave China, signaling potential shifts in U.S. manufacturing strategy. This move could impact global supply chains and trade dynamics. Meanwhile, the Federal Reserve faced pressure as the yield curve inverted briefly, raising concerns about the economy's vulnerability to recession. Fed Chair Jerome Powell emphasized progress toward maximum employment and price stability, but traders remained skeptical about aggressive easing. St. Louis Fed President James Bullard urged continued rate cuts, highlighting the risks of an inverted yield curve. These developments underscore the delicate balance the Fed must maintain amid geopolitical tensions and market demands.

summary: A new analysis by researchers at the University of California, Berkeley suggests that organic farming may be more drought-resistant than conventional farming. The study, which reviewed over 100 studies, found that organic farming creates a unique mix of biodiversity in the soil and surrounding environment that is difficult to mimic with synthetic chemicals. The findings were published in the journal the Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. The researchers found a productivity gap—organic farms are almost 20 percent less productive than conventional ones, a number still lower than conclusions drawn by many previous studies. However, the group also thinks that this gap could be reduced or even totally eliminated by further investment in organic farming research, education, and seed breeding. Claire Kremen, one of the researchers, said that with global food needs predicted to greatly increase in the next 50 years, it's critical to look more closely at organic farming because the ability of synthetic fertilizers to increase crop yields has been declining. The Rodale Institute's Farming Systems Trial, which has been comparing the productivity of organic and conventional farms since 1981, found that organic plots outperformed conventional ones, especially during droughts or other adverse weather conditions. Kristine Nichols, the chief scientist for the Rodale Institute, explained that the difference comes down to what is in the soil. The microbes, fungi, and other organisms that build up in organically farmed soil create mutually dependent relationships with plants, allowing the soil to absorb and store more water. This makes organic farming more resilient to droughts and other weather events. A report suggests that organic farming may be more drought-resistant than conventional methods, but the findings are contested. The report, authored by Miller and shared with CNBC, highlights that genetically engineered crops are widely adopted, with 18 million farmers in 27 countries using them last year. Miller notes the high 'repeat index' of farmers purchasing these seeds, such as those from Monsanto. However, some farmers, like Joel Nelson of the California Citrus Mutual, argue that organic farming has no impact on water usage. Nelson points out that organic producers typically yield 40% less than conventional ones but use the same amount of water. The report also questions whether the results from the Rodale farm, which is about 12 acres, can scale to larger operations. Kremen adds that converting the entire U.S. food system to organic would require significant economic, political, and structural changes, and the true cost of conventional agriculture includes hidden expenses like environmental damage and health issues. Currently, less than 2% of agricultural government funding goes to organic farming.

summary: On September 12, 2014, the U.S. Treasury announced expanded sanctions targeting Russian entities in the financial services, energy, and defense sectors. These measures were taken in response to Russia’s continued efforts to destabilize eastern Ukraine and its violation of Ukraine’s territorial integrity and sovereignty. The sanctions include freezing assets of designated firms and prohibiting transactions involving these entities. The targeted companies include OAO ‘Dolgoprudny Research Production Enterprise,’ Mytishchinski Mashinostroitelny Zavod, Kalinin Machine Plant JSC, Almaz-Antey GSKB, and JSC NIIP, all of which are involved in the production of weapons, ammunition, and defense systems. Additionally, the Treasury modified Directive 1 under E.O. 13662 to restrict U.S. persons and entities from engaging in transactions involving new debt with a maturity of more than 30 days for sanctioned financial institutions, including Sberbank of Russia, which is Russia’s largest financial institution. These measures aim to limit access to U.S. dollar financing and increase costs for the Russian government. The U.S. Treasury has imposed new sanctions and strengthened existing ones targeting Russian energy companies, including Gazprom, Gazprom Neft, Lukoil, Surgutneftegas, and Rosneft. These measures, under Executive Order 13662, prohibit U.S. persons and entities from providing goods, services, or technology to support exploration or production in deepwater, Arctic offshore, or shale projects in Russia. The sanctions aim to hinder Russia’s ability to develop unconventional oil resources, which rely heavily on U.S. and Western technology. While the measures do not interfere with current energy supply or prevent Russian companies from selling oil and gas, they limit long-term development of technically challenging projects. Gazprom Neft and Transneft have also been added to the prohibitions, with restrictions on financing and dealings in new debt over 90 days. On September 12, 2014, the U.S. Treasury announced expanded sanctions targeting Russian financial services, energy, and defense-related sectors. summary: In 2018, U.S. housing prices were rising faster than the rate of inflation, with some areas seeing increases three times higher. This trend was observed in both high-cost cities like Seattle and San Francisco, as well as lower-cost cities such as Charlotte and Tampa. The rapid increase in home prices was causing significant strain on the middle class, making it increasingly difficult for them to achieve the American dream of homeownership. Nationally, home prices were approaching the peak levels seen in 2006, just before the housing market collapsed into a foreclosure crisis and the economy plunged into the Great Recession. Major cities across the country, including Los Angeles, Washington, D.C., Cleveland, and Chicago, were all experiencing rising home prices, with some reaching or nearing historical highs.

Life insurance sales have increased significantly due to the coronavirus pandemic, with many firms reporting double-digit growth in policy sales compared to the previous year. This surge is attributed to heightened awareness of financial risks associated with mortality and a fear of death, as highlighted by experts. The increase is particularly notable among younger adults, who have been buying insurance in elevated numbers since the spring of 2020, when the pandemic began to impact the U.S. heavily. According to Limra, an insurance industry group, just over half of American adults reported having a life insurance policy in 2020, down from 63% a decade earlier. However, Google Search traffic for 'life insurance' jumped 50% between March and May 2020 compared to the same period in 2019. Northwestern Mutual, the nation's largest seller of life insurance, saw a 15% increase in policy sales between April and September 2020. Similarly, AccuQuote, an online insurance marketplace, reported a 30% growth in policy sales due to the pandemic. Jennifer Fitzgerald, CEO of Policygenius, noted that the pandemic has forced the idea of financial protection and mortality to the forefront of consumers' minds. Manoj Upreti, a senior life insurance analyst at Aite Group, mentioned that the increase is likely to continue in the second half of the year. Younger consumers, particularly those under 44, showed a 13% increase in life insurance applications in the third quarter of 2020 compared to Q3 2019, indicating a broader trend in the industry. Life insurance sales have increased during the coronavirus pandemic, with term insurance being particularly popular. Term insurance, which provides coverage for a set term (such as 10, 20, or 30 years), is more affordable and attractive to consumers amid economic uncertainty. Larry Rybka, chairman and CEO of Valmark Financial Group, noted that 90% of consumers need coverage for a specific period, such as to support their families or pay off mortgages. Valmark has seen a 25% increase in life insurance applications this year. Digital brokers like Haven Life Insurance Agency, owned by MassMutual, reported a 34% rise in policies sold during the second and third quarters of 2020 compared to the same period in 2019. The shift to digital interactions, driven by social distancing requirements, has also contributed to this trend. Online brokers typically do not require medical exams for term policies under $1 million, reducing in-person interactions. However, some insurers have raised premiums for new buyers, especially for longer-term policies, due to low interest rates making it harder to meet financial guarantees. Restrictions on underwriting have also affected certain high-risk groups, such as those over 60 with health issues.

title: Federal Reserve Board - Federal Reserve issues FOMC statement
summary: The Federal Reserve issued a FOMC statement on January 28, 2015, highlighting that economic activity has expanded at a solid pace. Labor market conditions improved further, with strong job gains and a lower unemployment rate. Household spending rose moderately, and recent energy price declines boosted purchasing power. Business fixed investment advanced, while the housing recovery remained slow. Inflation fell below the Committee’s longer-run objective, largely due to energy price declines. Market-based inflation compensation measures dropped significantly, while survey-based inflation expectations remained stable. The Fed reaffirmed its 0 to 1/4 percent federal funds rate target range and will assess progress toward its goals, including labor market conditions and inflation expectations, before beginning to normalize monetary policy. The Fed indicated that rate hikes may occur sooner if progress toward employment and inflation targets is faster than expected, or be delayed if progress is slower. The Fed also maintained its policy of reinvesting principal payments from agency debt and mortgage-backed securities, and rolling over maturing Treasury securities.

Spark Therapeutics' Luxturna, the first gene therapy approved in the U.S., is priced at $850,000 for a one-time treatment, or $425,000 per eye for a rare inherited retinal disease. The therapy, approved by the FDA in December 2017, targets a condition that can lead to blindness, affecting between 1,000 and 2,000 people in the U.S. Luxturna works by delivering a healthy copy of the RPE65 gene to restore vision. Clinical trials showed significant improvement in patients' ability to navigate obstacle courses in low light after a year. Spark also introduced payment and access programs, including outcomes-based pricing, where payments are tied to the therapy's effectiveness. The company aims to ensure access for patients by offering financial support and logistics for travel. Luxturna will be available at half a dozen treatment centers in the U.S. this year. Spark's CEO, Jeff Marrazzo, emphasized the importance of affordability and long-term durability of the therapy. Similar models are being used by other companies, such as Novartis with Kymriah, which offers refunds if the treatment is ineffective. Spark has partnered with Express Scripts to offer insurers a direct purchasing option for Luxturna, avoiding the 'buy and bill' model. This initiative aims to reduce financial risks for treatment centers and lower markup costs for insurers. Express Scripts, as a pharmacy benefit manager, will negotiate drug prices and reimbursement on behalf of insurers and employers. Spark is also exploring staggered payment options for expensive one-time treatments, though challenges include government price regulations and frequent insurance provider changes. The company is in discussions with the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to potentially waive some requirements, enabling installment payments and larger rebates based on treatment effectiveness. Miller from Express Scripts emphasized the need to innovate in drug payment models as more expensive treatments enter the market.

On February 5, 2016, the Federal Reserve Bank (FRB) released a FEDS Note titled 'State and Local Pension Funding in the Enhanced Financial Accounts.' This report introduces new state-level data on the funding status of state and local government defined-benefit (DB) pension plans, which is part of the Enhanced Financial Accounts (EFA) initiative. Previously, the Financial Accounts of the United States reported aggregate levels of pension assets and liabilities in Table L.120.b. The new EFA tables and maps provide annual state-level detail on pension assets, liabilities, and various measures of funding status, going back to 2000. State and local governments have traditionally offered DB plans, while the private sector has largely moved to defined-contribution (DC) plans. In 2013, state and local DB pension entitlements totaled $4.9 trillion, compared to $0.5 trillion in DC arrangements. The funding status of these plans has received increased attention due to underfunded plans and debates over liability measurement methods. The note highlights that pension liabilities are calculated using different discount rates, with lower rates leading to higher present values and a worse funding outlook. The Government Accounting Standards Board (GASB) guidelines use expected returns on pension assets to calculate liabilities, resulting in higher discount rates and better funding appearances. Research suggests that lower discount rates should be used to reflect the lower risk of pension obligations due to legal protections. According to the Center for Retirement Research, state and local pension funds were underfunded by about $1 trillion in 2014. The report also discusses the estimation of plan assets using data from the Census survey and the BEA discount rate, which has varied over time. The findings are based on data from 1997 to 2014, with some gaps in state-by-state breakdowns for specific years.

summary: Ulta Beauty is accelerating its curbside pickup and introducing same-day delivery to cater to consumers who have grown accustomed to online shopping during the pandemic. The company's financial outlook for fiscal 2022 through 2024 anticipates diluted earnings per share growth in the low double-digits, with capital expenditures between 4% and 5% of sales, translating to $1.1 billion to $1.4 billion. Ulta expects its net sales growth to outpace the broader beauty and personal care industry, with a target of 5% to 7% versus 2% to 4% for the rest of the industry. Same-store sales are projected to rise between 3% and 5% annually, with 50 new stores opening each year. However, shares fell over 10% on Tuesday due to the company's forecast falling short of investor expectations. The pandemic has significantly impacted the high-touch beauty industry, forcing retailers like Ulta to adapt by offering more digital and contactless services. Ulta added curbside pickup in April 2020 and saw a 17.9% decline in sales online and in stores open for at least 14 months during the fiscal year ended Jan. 30. Despite these challenges, Ulta's second-quarter same-store sales rose 56.3% compared to the year-ago period, indicating a rebound in consumer demand. Ulta Beauty is adapting to evolving consumer habits by emphasizing speedy delivery and digital engagement. The company is focusing on attracting more Black and Hispanic customers through an expanded assortment of textured-hair products. Ulta executives noted that some pandemic-related behaviors, such as self-care routines and increased interest in wellness-related beauty products, are likely to persist. Chief Operating Officer Kecia Steelman highlighted the blurring line between in-person and online shopping, with customers using TikTok videos to inspire purchases and later visiting stores for in-person experiences. Chief Digital Officer Prama Bhatt emphasized that customers who shop across both channels spend significantly more and make more purchases annually. In response, Ulta plans to roll out same-day delivery in select markets ahead of the holidays, though details on fees and availability remain undisclosed. The company also aims to have curbside pickup orders ready within two hours. Competitor Sephora has already launched same-day delivery in major cities with a flat fee of $6.95.

summary: DISH Network Corporation, through its subsidiary American H Block Wireless L.L.C., filed an application with the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to acquire all 176 H Block wireless spectrum licenses in Auction 96. The FCC's prohibition on certain communications related to the Auction expired on March 14, 2014. American won all 176 H Block Licenses with an aggregate bid of $1.564 billion, which concluded on February 27, 2014. However, the FCC has not issued the licenses yet, as the issuance depends on its review and approval of the application. DISH paid approximately $328 million to the FCC as a deposit on December 17, 2013, and the remaining balance of approximately $1.236 billion is due on March 28, 2014. If the FCC issues the licenses, DISH will also need to pay approximately $12.6 million to UTAM, Inc. and $94.9 million to Sprint Corporation for clearance costs. The 8-K filing by DISH Network Corporation on March 18, 2014, outlines the terms and conditions of the H Block Licenses, which are subject to specific build-out requirements. The licensee must provide signal coverage and offer service to at least 40% of the population in each area covered by an individual H Block License within four years of the FCC issuing the licenses. This is known as the H Block Interim Build-Out Requirement. If the licensee fails to meet this requirement, the license term and the H Block Final Build-Out Requirement may be accelerated by two years for each H Block License area in which it fails. The H Block Final Build-Out Requirement mandates that the licensee provide service to at least 75% of the population in each area covered by an individual H Block License within ten years. If the licensee fails to meet this requirement, its authorization for each H Block License area may terminate. The filing also highlights the potential need for significant investments or partnerships to finance the commercialization and build-out of any acquired H Block Licenses, as well as integration efforts and compliance with applicable regulations. The uncertainty surrounding the development and implementation of a business model for these licenses could affect the carrying value of potential assets and future financial condition.

summary: On July 23, 2014, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) adopted amendments to the rules governing money market mutual funds. The reforms aim to address run risks while preserving the benefits of these funds. The new rules require institutional prime money market funds to use a floating net asset value (NAV), allowing daily share prices to fluctuate with market conditions. Additionally, the rules introduce liquidity fees and redemption gates to manage periods of stress. The reforms also include enhanced diversification, disclosure, and stress testing requirements. A two-year transition period is provided for funds and investors to adjust. The SEC also proposed exemptions from certain confirmation requirements and re-proposed amendments to address credit rating references under the Dodd-Frank Act. The rules will take effect 60 days after publication in the Federal Register. The SEC introduced new tools, such as fees and gates, to address potential liquidity crises by allowing fund boards to impose liquidity fees or temporarily suspend redemptions if liquidity levels fall below a threshold. Additionally, the reforms include enhanced diversification, disclosure, and stress testing requirements, as well as updated reporting standards for funds operating similarly to money market funds. The U.S. Treasury and IRS will release tax guidance to support the implementation of these rules, including a simplified tax accounting method and relief from wash sale rules for floating NAV funds. These reforms follow the 2010 amendments, which aimed to improve the resilience of money market funds after the 2008 financial crisis, and are part of ongoing efforts to address potential risks in the financial system.

On May 6, 2015, the U.S. Department of the Treasury announced it would offer $64 billion in Treasury securities to refund approximately $67 billion in maturing Treasury notes due on May 15, 2015. This action is expected to result in a debt pay down of about $3 billion. The refunding includes a $24 billion 3-year note maturing on May 15, 2018; a $24 billion 10-year note maturing on May 15, 2025; and a $16 billion 30-year bond maturing on May 15, 2045. These securities will be auctioned on May 12, 13, and 14, 2015, with settlements on May 15, 2015. The Treasury also outlined plans to meet remaining financing needs through various auctions and operations, including a test buyback operation conducted on April 16, 2015. The Treasury plans to maintain current coupon issuance levels and adjust as needed based on projected financing needs. Additionally, the Treasury will increase the supply of Treasury bills to enhance market functioning and liquidity, while maintaining its strategy to extend the weighted average maturity of the debt. The Treasury also stated its intention to hold a cash balance sufficient to cover one week of outflows, subject to a minimum balance of $150 billion, as part of its updated cash management policy. The U.S. Department of the Treasury issued a statement on May 6, 2015, regarding the debt limit and the government's ability to meet its obligations. The debt limit does not authorize new spending but allows the government to finance existing legal obligations. The Temporary Debt Limit Extension Act suspended the debt limit through March 15, 2015. Since March 16, the U.S. has reached its statutory debt limit. The Treasury suspended the sale of State and Local Government Series securities to avoid exceeding the limit. Congress did not act to raise the debt limit, so the Treasury implemented extraordinary measures to continue financing the government. These measures provide temporary headroom under the debt limit. The Treasury emphasized that Congress is responsible for extending the nation’s borrowing authority and urged Congress to raise the debt limit as soon as possible. The next quarterly refunding announcement was scheduled for August 5, 2015.

The U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) reported that real gross domestic product (GDP) increased by 1.1 percent in the second quarter of 2016, according to the second estimate released on August 26, 2016. This growth rate was 0.1 percentage point less than the advance estimate from July. In the first quarter, real GDP rose by 0.8 percent. The increase in real GDP was primarily driven by higher consumer spending, particularly on nondurable goods like food and beverage items, durable goods such as recreational goods and vehicles, and services including housing, utilities, and healthcare. However, the growth was partially offset by a decline in inventory investment, with GDP less inventory investment (real final sales of domestic product) increasing by 2.4 percent. Other factors that partially offset GDP growth included declines in housing investment, state and local government spending, and business investment. The downward revision to the second estimate of GDP growth mainly reflected downward revisions to state and local government spending and inventory investment, as well as an upward revision to imports. Corporate profits decreased by 1.2 percent in the second quarter of 2016 after rising 3.4 percent in the first quarter.

summary: Treasury Secretary Janet L. Yellen addressed inquiries from State Attorneys General about the implementation of Section 9901 of the American Rescue Plan Act. The provision provides funds to States, territories, Tribal governments, and localities to manage the economic consequences of the pandemic. Congress has given States considerable flexibility to use the funds but has also placed limitations to ensure the money is used for its intended purposes. Specifically, the Act prohibits using the funds to offset a reduction in net tax revenue from certain state law changes. Yellen emphasized that the Act does not prevent States from enacting a broad variety of tax cuts, as long as the funds are not used to offset those cuts. Treasury is developing further guidance to clarify the implementation of the provision and will provide it before states must submit a certification under § 602(d)(1). The letter was sent on March 23, 2021, and was circulated to multiple state officials, including those from Arizona, West Virginia, Massachusetts, and others. In today's housing market, renting has become a more attractive option compared to buying. According to Realtor.com, the monthly costs of buying and owning a home have increased by 14% over the past year, which is more than three times the annual increase in rent rates nationally. Rents have only risen by 4% during the same period. This shift has made renting a more cost-effective and potentially wealth-building option for many. Research from Florida Atlantic University and Florida International University indicates that renting and reinvesting the savings can outperform owning and building home equity in terms of wealth creation. This trend has been driven by fast-rising home prices and higher mortgage rates, which have made buying more expensive. While buying is still more favorable in certain regions like the Midwest and Northeast, the overall trend suggests that renting may be a better investment in many major metropolitan areas. In today's housing market, renting is often a more favorable option than buying, according to Hale, chief economist at realtor.com. The shift in demand from buying to renting is expected to cool overheated home prices. This trend is already evident, as the supply of homes for sale in July was flat compared to the previous year, marking the first time in several years. While home prices are still rising, the pace has slowed, indicating that sellers are beginning to see a decline in demand as buyers face affordability challenges. William Hardin, director of Florida International's Jerome Bain Real Estate Institute, noted that interest rates are low, and there are few junk mortgages available. Additionally, employment, income, and borrower credit ratings are all improving, which are positive signs for a smoother transition in the housing market.

The U.S. Department of the Treasury, along with the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), has made financial inclusion a key policy priority, resulting in significant progress over the past eight years. In the United States, the unbanked rate fell by 15 percent between 2011 and 2015, reaching a historic low of 7 percent. Globally, the number of adults without access to formal financial services dropped by 20 percent from 2.5 billion to 2.0 billion between 2011 and 2014. These gains were driven by strong partnerships among governments, private sector actors, and nonprofits. New technologies, such as mobile phones and the Internet, have further expanded opportunities to bring more people into the formal financial system. Four new initiatives were announced to build on this progress, including the Financial Inclusion Fellows program, India’s first cashless city, the Digital Development Advisor Program, and an updated National Strategy for Financial Literacy. The administration has also invested in community development financial institutions (CDFIs), which have expanded services to 43,000 consumers and made 58,000 small-dollar loans. The CDFI Program invested $1.1 billion over six years, contributing to over $14 billion in loans and investments. The initiative also prioritized financial inclusion in global forums like the G-20 and launched myRA, a retirement savings account for those without employer-sponsored plans. The Barcelona Principles were established to ensure humanitarian cash aid via digital payments supports long-term recovery. The Office of Technical Assistance (OTA) is working in eight countries to develop financial inclusion strategies and modernize financial infrastructure. In 2016, CDFI awardees provided 23,000 small-dollar loans and opened 3,741 Individual Development Accounts. USAID supported cash preparedness through grants to Mercy Corps and CRS, focusing on digital cash transfers. The Financial Empowerment Innovation Fund invested $6.2 million in research to improve financial health. The Better than Cash Alliance (BTCA), co-founded by USAID, now includes 24 national governments and other organizations. USAID also made e-payments the default method for development assistance, leading to significant efficiency gains in Bangladesh. The frozen yogurt franchise industry has experienced significant growth, with companies like Red Mango and TCBY expanding their presence across the U.S. Despite the industry's growth, analysts predict a slowdown in the coming years due to market saturation. Red Mango, which has over 160 open locations and plans for 160 to 200 more, is optimistic about the future of the frozen yogurt market. The company focuses on health-conscious consumers and has adopted a franchise model to expand efficiently. However, the industry faces challenges in retaining customers and maintaining profitability, with smaller players struggling to stay afloat. TCBY, the largest player in the market, has seen fluctuations in profitability over the years, highlighting the competitive nature of the frozen yogurt industry. The frozen yogurt franchise market has seen significant growth, with companies like TCBY and Menchie’s expanding their operations. Greg Allison, TCBY’s senior director of marketing, insights and innovation, noted that competition in the frozen yogurt space has increased over the past few years. Despite this, TCBY plans to add about 100 stores in the U.S. and 20 to 30 internationally. The company credits its recent growth to a rebranding strategy, including a new logo and self-service options. Menchie’s, which currently has 165 open locations and 246 in development, also aims for extensive expansion. The CEO of Menchie’s, Amit Kleinberger, highlighted the role of price in frozen yogurt’s popularity, noting that the company thrived during the recession. IBISWorld analysts found that the recent economic climate has actually benefited frozen yogurt sales, as consumers indulge in inexpensive luxuries during tough times. However, Riggs pointed out that price remains a challenge for stores trying to encourage repeat buyers.

Net premiums earned rose by 14% to $2,784.4 million. However, net income attributable to Progressive decreased by 36% to $175.9 million from $274.7 million in the same period last year. The per share available to common shareholders also dropped by 36% to $0.30 from $0.46. The company's combined ratio increased slightly to 93.4 from 92.3. Policies in force for personal lines grew by 11% to 19,066.9, with a 12% increase in direct auto policies. The company also reported a 10% increase in companywide total policies in force to 21,935.9. The financial results for The Progressive Corporation and its subsidiaries for the period ending August 2019 show a net income attributable to Progressive of $2,618.6 million, compared to $2,100.6 million in the prior year. The company also reported comprehensive income attributable to Progressive of $3,381.7 million, reflecting a significant increase from $1,931.7 million in the previous year. The GAAP ratios for the company include a loss/LAE ratio of 72.7%, an expense ratio of 18.7%, and a combined ratio of 91.4%. These figures indicate the company's performance in managing its underwriting and operational costs. The report also highlights the impact of actuarial adjustments on the financial results, particularly for the Property business, where the loss/LAE ratio was influenced by favorable reinsurance recoverables and amortization expenses. The company's investment results show a fully taxable equivalent (FTE) total return of 0.9% for the total portfolio, with fixed-income securities yielding 1.2% and common stocks returning (1.9)%.

On November 21, 2019, Deputy Secretary Muzinich of the U.S. Department of the Treasury delivered a keynote address at the TCH + BPI 2019 Annual Conference in New York, NY. The speech covered financial regulatory reform, economic policy and national security, and the evolving financial services landscape. Muzinich noted that over 60% of proposed regulatory changes have been implemented. He highlighted the bipartisan banking reform bill S.2155, which became law in 2018, and the rules for enhanced prudential standards for U.S. and foreign-owned banks. The Volcker Rule was reformed, with community banks under $10 billion in assets generally exempted. Tax reform, including the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017, was discussed, focusing on lowering corporate tax rates, moving to a territorial tax system, and allowing immediate expensing of capital equipment. Muzinich emphasized the importance of rising wages for economic growth and the role of capital investment in productivity. Business investment has grown significantly, with intellectual property investment increasing at 7.8% annually since the tax reform enactment, compared to 4.9% over the previous four years. Research and development spending grew at 6.7% versus 3.5%. Real hourly wages rose 1.9% for the 12 months ending September 2019, compared to 0.4% from 2009 to 2016. The administration added an average of 174,000 jobs per month, surpassing the Congressional Budget Office's projection of 25,000 new jobs per month in 2019. Unemployment remained at 3.6%, with historically low rates for African Americans, Hispanic Americans, and women. Over 7 million Americans were lifted off food stamps since the election. Muzinich also discussed the intersection of economic policy and national security, emphasizing the use of sanctions, CFIUS, and AML reforms to protect national interests. He emphasized the need to modernize the AML regime, noting the U.S. has one of the strongest AML systems globally but acknowledges the necessity for reform under the Bank Secrecy Act. Beneficial ownership reforms are a priority, as the U.S. permits the creation of anonymous shell corporations without disclosing ownership. The Treasury aims to identify ultimate owners at company formation to prevent illicit activities such as terrorist financing. The challenge lies in balancing national security, small business needs, and privacy. The speech also addressed the evolving financial landscape, including the impact of technology on payments, deposits, and credit. Non-bank entities like PayPal and SoFi are offering services traditionally provided by banks. Cryptocurrencies are highlighted as a significant trend with implications for national security and regulatory frameworks. Muzinich emphasized the importance of AML and countering the financing of terrorism in the context of digital currencies. He noted that U.S. laws apply equally to transactions in both traditional fiat currency and digital currency. However, the potential for cryptocurrencies to enable anonymous transactions raises concerns about law enforcement challenges. Muzinich also discussed the broader implications of digital currencies on monetary policy, financial stability, and user privacy. He referenced historical context, noting that in the 1830s, 90% of U.S. currency was issued by private entities, but this system was ultimately replaced by a centralized financial framework. Muzinich raised questions about the governance of large-scale digital currencies, including who would make decisions about their regulation and whether such decisions would remain in the hands of elected officials. He concluded by reaffirming the U.S. Treasury's commitment to balancing innovation with regulatory oversight to protect the public interest.

title: Speech by Vice Chair Yellen on revolution and evolution in central bank communications - Federal Reserve Board
summary: On November 13, 2012, Federal Reserve Vice Chair Yellen emphasized the importance of clear communication in central bank policy, highlighting its role in enhancing the effectiveness of monetary policy. She noted that the financial crisis underscored the necessity of transparency, leading to significant advancements in communication strategies. The Fed is utilizing unconventional tools, including large-scale asset purchases and forward guidance, to stimulate economic recovery. These efforts are part of the Federal Open Market Committee's (FOMC) response to the current economic environment, where traditional policy tools are constrained. Yellen outlined the FOMC's forward guidance, emphasizing continued purchase of mortgage-backed securities (MBS) and other assets until labor market conditions improve, maintaining a highly accommodative monetary policy stance for an extended period, and keeping federal funds rates exceptionally low through mid-2015. Yellen also emphasized the importance of maintaining consistent principles in central bank communications, with the FOMC aiming to reaffirm its consensus statement annually, focusing on a 2 percent inflation goal measured by the PCE price index. This goal is paired with a specific employment target, reflecting a balanced approach to managing inflation and employment deviations.

summary: Mobile payments have not gained significant traction in the U.S., despite the widespread use of smartphones. Experts attribute this to entrenched legacy systems, the prevalence of rewards cards, and a lack of demand for alternative payment methods. In contrast, countries like China and India have seen rapid adoption of mobile payments, with over 80% of Chinese consumers using mobile payments in 2018. In the U.S., adoption rates for major mobile payment apps remain below 10%. The U.S. is considered to be in the middle of the pack globally when it comes to mobile payments. The credit and debit card system is well-established and continues to dominate the payment landscape. In India, regulators have pushed for a shift to digital payments to increase tax revenue, while in China, tech giants like Alibaba and Tencent have driven the adoption of mobile payments by competing for customers' wallets. These factors have contributed to the slower adoption of mobile payments in the U.S. Mobile payments have struggled to gain traction in the U.S. due to the widespread use of credit and debit cards, which are already deeply embedded in the payment ecosystem. According to Arieh Levi of CB Insights, the high saturation of cards in the U.S. and Europe means people already have a digital payment method that doesn't involve cash. This makes it harder for mobile payment solutions to gain momentum. Additionally, legacy players like Visa, Mastercard, and banks have a lot to lose if the status quo changes, as they rely on the revenue from card swipes. The economics of the industry are expected to remain the same, but the user experience will shift to smartphones. Merchants also face challenges in adopting mobile payment systems, as it requires significant investment in hardware and infrastructure. While there are several mobile payment options available, such as Apple Pay, Google Pay, and Samsung Pay, their adoption remains limited. The Starbucks app is an exception, with 23.4 million users, showing that mobile payments can succeed in specific use cases. However, widespread adoption is still far off, as merchants need at least 90% acceptance before consumers will consider switching to mobile payments. Mobile payments have not gained significant traction in the U.S., despite the rise of digital wallets like Apple Pay and Google Pay. Apple's new credit card with Goldman Sachs aims to drive liquidity into its mobile app ecosystem by offering cashback rewards for transactions made through Apple Pay. The card also provides higher rewards for purchases made directly through Apple. Meanwhile, the Federal Reserve's real-time payments system, FedNow Service, could reshape the mobile payment landscape by enabling instant money transfers. This could allow companies like PayPal and tech giants such as Facebook and Amazon to offer more bank-like services through mobile platforms. However, credit cards are expected to remain relevant due to their rewards, borrowing capabilities, and the preference for non-immediate payments. The future of mobile payments may involve hybrid models that integrate traditional card features into digital platforms.

The United States has launched a new plan to challenge China's dominance in the rare earth metals market, which is critical for electric vehicles, renewable energy systems, and advanced technology manufacturing. According to the U.S. Geological Survey, China accounted for 80% of rare earth imports in 2019, although exports declined in 2020 due to the impact of the pandemic. The Biden administration has prioritized rare earths as part of its domestic supply chain strategy, with significant investments planned in climate and technology initiatives. The Department of Energy announced a $30 million initiative to secure the U.S. supply chain for rare earths and other battery materials like cobalt and lithium. The U.S. has previously attempted to reestablish itself as a major player in the rare earths market, but challenges remain in scaling up processing and refining capabilities to compete with China's established dominance. The MP Materials rare earth mine in Mountain Pass, California, is one of the key sites in this effort. The U.S. faces technical, environmental, and political hurdles in rebuilding its rare earths industry, especially in the short term. The U.S. is taking steps to reduce its reliance on China for rare earth metals, which are critical for defense, technology, and electric vehicles. Neodymium and praseodymium are among the most sought-after light rare earth elements, essential for motors, turbines, and medical devices. Demand for these materials has surged with the growth of technology and the expansion of the electric vehicle market. While China currently dominates the market, the U.S. held a majority stake before the 1980s. Production shifted overseas due to environmental pressures and cheaper labor costs. The Department of Defense has noted that China strategically flooded the market with cheaper rare earths to deter competitors. Companies without diversified supply chains face risks of scarcity and rising prices. MP Materials, based in Las Vegas, is working to restore the U.S. rare earth supply chain, from mine to magnet, and is seeking to become the lowest-cost producer. The company has received significant government funding and is planning to expand domestic refining capabilities by 2025. Lynas Corporation, an Australian company, is also investing in U.S. rare earth processing facilities with support from the Pentagon. The United States is pursuing a strategy to reduce its reliance on China's dominance in the rare earth metals market, aiming to create competitive markets and meet the rising demand for 21st-century technologies. Companies like Lynas and MP Materials are working to expand domestic supply chains, but the extraction of rare earths faces challenges due to environmental, technical, and political factors. The U.S. is also exploring alternatives to mining, such as recycling old batteries and disk drives. Companies like Redwood Materials and Li-Cycle are leading efforts in battery recycling, while the Ames Laboratory is researching eco-friendly methods to recover rare earths. Despite these initiatives, the U.S. faces limitations in countering China's influence, as China accounts for about 30% of global carbon dioxide emissions and has invested significantly in energy transition. John Kerry emphasized that the focus is on global cooperation rather than a direct rivalry with China. The United States is planning to challenge China's dominance in the rare earth metals market, which is crucial for electric vehicles (EVs). According to data from IHS Markit, EV sales are expected to reach 12.2 million by 2025, driving up demand for raw materials. However, building a domestic supply chain would require "massive levels of production" and could take up to a decade. title: Federal Reserve Board - Federal Reserve Board adopts final rule to strengthen the ability of government authorities to resolve in orderly way largest domestic and foreign banks operating in the United States
summary: On December 15, 2016, the Federal Reserve Board adopted a final rule to enhance the capacity of government authorities to resolve the failure of the largest domestic and foreign banks operating in the United States in an orderly manner. The rule applies to domestic firms designated as global systemically important banks (GSIBs) and the U.S. operations of foreign GSIBs. The objective is to minimize the systemic impact of a GSIB failure by imposing losses on investors rather than taxpayers, while ensuring critical operations continue. This is achieved by requiring GSIBs to maintain sufficient long-term debt that can be converted to equity during resolution, thereby providing a source of private capital to support the firm's operations. The rule mandates that long-term debt must survive the loss of a bank's equity and subsequent failure, and be convertible into new equity. Debt issued on or before December 31, 2016, will be grandfathered, allowing it to count toward a firm's long-term debt requirements despite certain contractual clauses. Debt issued after this date must fully comply with the rule. All firms are required to adhere to the rule by January 1, 2019.

summary: Thermo Fisher Scientific launched the Ion Torrent Genexus System, a next-generation sequencing (NGS) platform that delivers results in a single day. summary: On July 20, 2012, President Obama signed an Executive Order (E.O.) titled 'Taking Additional Steps to Address the National Emergency with Respect to Somalia.' This E.O. expands the U.S. Department of the Treasury's authority to sanction individuals and entities contributing to the security deterioration and violence in Somalia. The order targets those misappropriating Somali public assets, recruiting children as soldiers, and committing acts of violence against Somali civilians. It also prohibits the importation of charcoal from Somalia into the U.S., a significant revenue source for al-Shabaab, a U.S.-designated Foreign Terrorist Organization. The U.S. aims to reduce al-Shabaab's revenue and environmental degradation linked to charcoal production, which exacerbates the humanitarian crisis in the Horn of Africa. The order grants the authority to target individuals who may jeopardize the security situation in Somalia. This action is part of broader efforts to enhance security and stability in the region. The U.S. Department of the Treasury plays a key role in implementing these measures, reflecting the government's commitment to addressing the crisis through targeted actions.

Ford is implementing five major strategies to address its struggling international operations. summary: Zambia's spiraling debt and the future of Chinese loan financing in Africa have become a focal point of global financial discussions. China has provided billions of dollars in loans for infrastructure projects across Sub-Saharan Africa, with Zambia being one of the most prominent debtors. Recent research from EXX Africa indicates that Chinese firms are seeking control of Zambian mining assets as collateral for potential loan defaults. Zambia is currently restructuring, renegotiating, or refinancing its extensive Chinese project finance debt, but Chinese companies are showing little patience and are instead seeking fresh collateral in case of default. The country's sovereign debt is expected to reach 96% of GDP in 2020, and it has defaulted on a spree of loans in 2019, including a $107 million loan from Italian bank Intesa Sanpaolo. The International Monetary Fund has withheld credit facilities due to concerns over Zambia's high debt and shrinking foreign exchange reserves. Zambian GDP has halved to just 2% over the past three years, and the kwacha currency has depreciated by almost 17% against the dollar. President Edgar Lungu has stated that his government will seek to reduce domestic arrears and maintain debt within sustainable levels. Chinese financial institutions are increasingly seeking control over Zambian mining assets as collateral for loans. Chinese companies, including China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation, are reportedly seeking restructuring of loan agreements that could involve mining assets being placed as collateral. Negotiations are likely being conducted by China Exim Bank, Sinosure (China Export & Credit Corporation), and Chinese government officials. Additionally, China retains a highly contentious stake in Zambia's national broadcaster, ZNBC. In 2017, Chinese media conglomerate StarTimes funded the rollout of a migration to a new digital TV signal and now controls 60% of a joint digital venture with ZNBC, called TopStar. The venture was also bankrolled by a $232 million loan from Exim Bank and has been criticized by media watchdogs for allegedly granting excessive influence over the media landscape to Beijing. Zambian government representatives did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Sinosure, Exim Bank, and China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation have also been contacted for comment.

Cohn, who opposes the tariffs, had previously been in a disagreement with Trump over trade policies, and the administration delayed the announcement initially. The decision was made after a meeting with key advisors, including Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross and trade advisor Peter Navarro, who supported the measures. Cohn's globalist views, which are a counterweight to Trump's protectionist policies, remain a point of contention within the administration.

summary: LKQ Corporation, a leading provider of alternative vehicle replacement products, operates through three segments: Wholesale—North America, Wholesale—Europe, and Self Service. The company distributes a variety of products to collision and mechanical repair shops, including aftermarket, recycled, refurbished, and remanufactured items. LKQ is the largest provider of alternative vehicle collision replacement products in the U.S. and a leading provider of mechanical replacement products in the U.K. and Canada. The company sources most of its aftermarket inventory from U.S., Taiwan, European, and Chinese manufacturers. Recycled products are obtained by purchasing salvaged vehicles and dismantling them. LKQ also sells refurbished and remanufactured products like wheels, bumper covers, lights, and engines. The company's primary customers are collision and mechanical repair shops, with indirect reliance on insurance companies to drive demand. LKQ has pursued growth through acquisitions, including 16 during the nine months ended September 30, 2013, with significant investments in European and North American markets. title: Novo Nordisk Receives FDA Approval of OZEMPIC® (semaglutide) Injection For the Treatment of Adults with Type 2 Diabetes
summary: Novo Nordisk received FDA approval for OZEMPIC® (semaglutide) injection in December 2017 for treating adults with type 2 diabetes. The drug is indicated as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control. OZEMPIC® is a GLP-1 analog with a long half-life, suitable for once-weekly dosing. It stimulates insulin and lowers glucagon secretion in a glucose-dependent manner. The approval comes with warnings about potential serious side effects, including thyroid tumors and cancer. Rodent studies suggest the drug may cause thyroid tumors, including thyroid cancer, though it is not known if it will cause medull, thyroid carcinoma (MTC) in humans. Patients with a history of MTC or Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2) should not use the drug. Allergies to semaglutide or ingredients in OZEMPIC® are also contraindications.

title: Deloitte Corporate Finance LLC Advises AirBorn, Inc. on its Financing with Goldman Sachs Specialty Lending Group
summary: Deloitte Corporate Finance LLC advised AirBorn, Inc. on its financing with Goldman Sachs Specialty Lending Group. The transaction aimed to provide liquidity for shareholder-related matters and flexibility for corporate growth initiatives. DCF leveraged its ESOP experience to analyze the Company's future cash needs, including obligations related to its S-Corp ESOP structure and synthetic equity positions. The deal supports AirBorn's strategy to enhance financial flexibility and capitalize on growth opportunities. AirBorn, Inc. secured financing through Goldman Sachs Specialty Lending Group, advised by Deloitte Corporate Finance LLC. The transaction involved a junior security, leveraging Deloit, ESOP advisory experience. AirBorn, an employee-owned manufacturer, operates in aerospace, defense, medical, industrial automation, and energy sectors.
