Most Americans want another stimulus check, but several factors are preventing its implementation. Republicans are concerned about the costs of sending out more stimulus checks, while some Democrats question the strategy. Despite these concerns, the possibility of additional cash payments is not entirely dead. The $1,200 payments from the CARES Act are likely already gone for many Americans. The Federal Reserve estimates the unemployment rate could exceed 30%. House Democrats passed a $3 trillion stimulus bill that would have given $1,200 to each American earning less than $75,000 annually, but President Trump called it 'dead on arrival.' Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell has called for a 'pause' in new relief funding. Critics argue that stimulus checks are poorly targeted and not stimulative, as they often go to people who are still employed and do not need the money. Instead, Republicans have supported a proposal to cut payroll taxes. Meanwhile, some Democrats suggest that strengthening unemployment benefits would provide more meaningful relief. Although the possibility of more cash payments is not dead, there is still uncertainty about its implementation. Larry Harris, a finance professor at the University of Southern California Marshall School of Business, believes that Trump will remain influential due to his substantial power over Republican funding, and that a strong economy will help his reelection efforts. This suggests that he will call for more stimulus checks. Felicia Wong, president and CEO of the Roosevelt Institute, also supports the idea of stimulus checks, stating that the suddenness and depth of the financial crisis necessitate unemployment benefits and cash payments. However, the unemployment system varies across states, and many agencies are short on staff and funds, leading to delays in the distribution of checks. A majority of GOP respondents, 53%, approve of more money going directly to Americans, according to a CNBC/Change Research poll. This public support is likely to find more reflection in Congress as the economic fallout of the pandemic continues.

summary: President Donald Trump, who has called himself the 'King of Debt,' has expressed a desire to wipe out Puerto Rico's debt, but experts say this is unlikely. Bond strategists indicate that Congress has already initiated a restructuring process, and it is improbable that this will be altered. While Trump's focus on the island may result in additional government loans, these would likely carry more weight than existing debt. Puerto Rico's bonds experienced a sharp decline following Trump's comments, with the benchmark general obligation bonds trading at 36 cents on the dollar. Bondholders, already anticipating a restructuring of the $72 billion debt, may now face an even larger loss. Congress has allocated some funds for Puerto Rico as part of hurricane relief, and the White House has requested more. Puerto Rico's current debt-to-GDP ratio is about 68 percent, compared to the average of 17 percent for U.S. states. The restructuring process is moving through the Title 3 bankruptcy framework, which was approved by Congress. Experts believe the restructuring may take several years due to the complexity of the situation and the impact of Hurricane Maria on the island's economy. Trump cannot completely wipe away Puerto Rico's debt, as the commonwealth constitution clearly states that bondholders must be paid first, even before pension beneficiaries. Some strategists believe Congress would not have much appetite to remove Puerto Rico's obligations, even if Trump wanted to. Approximately 25 percent of the island's general obligation bonds are insured, as are 70 percent of its COFINA sales tax bonds. The stocks of bond insurance companies, such as MBIA, were under pressure, with MBIA down about 9 percent. Strategists noted that it's not just hedge funds that will be affected by a haircut, as the majority of debt holders are individuals and mutual funds. Trump did not acknowledge individual holders in his comments on the debt. Lipton pointed out that White House Budget Director Mick Mulvaney emphasized that Trump's comments should not be taken literally, and the federal government will not bail out the debt.

summary: On October 15, 2018, U.S. Treasury Secretary Steven T. Mnuchin and Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Director Mick Mulvaney released details of the fiscal year (FY) 2018 budget results. The FY 2018 deficit was $779 billion, $113 billion higher than the previous year but $70 billion less than the FY 2019 Mid-Session Review (MSR) forecast. As a percentage of GDP, the deficit was 3.9%, up from 3.5% in FY 2017. The administration attributed the economic growth to the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) and a renewed focus on economic freedom, citing record job growth, increased consumer confidence, and a 2.9% real GDP growth over the past four quarters. The FY 2018 deficit was $54 billion less than the FY 2019 Budget estimate and $70 billion less than the MSR estimate. The administration emphasized the need for fiscal restraint and proposed measures to reduce the deficit by $3.6 trillion over 10 years. Total government receipts for FY 2018 amounted to $3,329 billion, an increase of $14 billion compared to FY 2017, representing a 0.4 percent rise. This was $6.8 billion above the Mid-Session Review (MSR) estimate. Receipts as a percentage of GDP were 16.5 percent, lower than the 17.2 percent in FY 2017 and below the 40-year average. The increase in receipts was primarily due to higher net individual income tax receipts, excise taxes, social insurance and retirement receipts, and customs duties, partially offset by lower net corporation income tax receipts and other factors. Outlays for FY 2018 totaled $4,108 billion, a 3.2 percent increase from FY 2017, with outlays as a percentage of GDP at 20.3 percent, slightly lower than the previous year and the 40-year average of 20.6 percent. The increase in outlays was attributed to higher spending on defense, Medicaid, Social Security, disaster relief, and other programs. Total Federal borrowing from the public increased by $1,084 billion to $15,751 billion, with borrowing as a percentage of GDP rising from 76.1 percent to 78.0 percent. The report highlighted several key areas where actual spending and receipts deviated from the initial projections. Lower-than-expected interest payments to credit financing accounts and higher-than-anticipated interest receipts contributed to a $9.3 billion difference. The Affordable Care Act’s Premium Tax Credits were $3.1 billion higher than projected due to increased enrollment in Health Insurance Exchanges. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) reported net outlays of -$15.9 billion, $4.0 billion lower than the initial estimate, driven by changes in the Deposit Insurance Fund. The U.S. Postal Service also saw net outlays of -$1.4 billion, attributed to higher receipts and lower expenses. The Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) reported a $1.4 billion surplus due to favorable weather, cost reductions, and lower interest rates. These results reflect the impact of various factors, including delayed appropriations and hurricane responses, on federal spending.

In 2019, the retail industry faced a wave of bankruptcies, with companies like Forever 21, Barneys New York, Sugarfina, and Destination Maternity filing for bankruptcy. Some retailers, such as Z Gallerie and Charming Charlie, returned to bankruptcy court for the second time, while others, like Fred's, liquidated their businesses entirely. Vince Tibone, a retail analyst, noted that 2019 was another significant year for retail bankruptcies, following 2017 and 2018. The apparel category was particularly affected, with numerous clothing retailers like Charlotte Russe, Diesel, A'Gaci, and Forever 21 filing for bankruptcy. This trend followed the department store bankruptcies of Sears and Bon-Ton in 2018. The shift in consumer behavior, with shoppers turning to platforms like Rent the Runway and Stitch Fix, or to stores like Target and TJ Maxx, contributed to the decline of traditional department stores. According to CB Insights, there were 23 retail bankruptcies in 2019, compared to 17 in 2018, with a total of 81 retail bankruptcies tracked since 2015. In 2019, the retail industry faced significant challenges as several major retailers filed for bankruptcy. Shopko, a discount retail business, filed for bankruptcy in January, initially hoping to salvage some of its locations but ultimately liquidating all of its assets, including over 300 stores. Gymboree, which filed for bankruptcy for the second time in January, announced plans to shutter all 800 of its stores but later found buyers for its brands. Things Remembered, a popular gifting chain, filed for bankruptcy in February and was sold to Enesco, which planned to save fewer than half of its 450 stores. Payless Shoesource, which filed for bankruptcy for the second time in February, announced the closure of over 2,000 stores across North America. Charlotte Russe, a teen apparel retailer, also filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in February, signaling the ongoing struggles of the retail sector during this period. In 2019, the retail industry faced significant challenges as several well-known brands filed for bankruptcy. Forever 21, a popular fast-fashion brand, was among those affected, with its brand and intellectual property sold to North American fashion house YM. YM planned to keep dozens of Charlotte Russe locations open. Diesel, another brand, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in March, citing sinking sales and expensive real estate deals as reasons for its financial struggles. Z Gallerie, a home furnishings retailer, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy for the second time, attributing its struggles to being late to invest in e-commerce. Roberto Cavalli, a luxury fashion brand, filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy in April, liquidating its entire North American business after losing its chief creative director. Charming Charlie, a youthful apparel brand, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in July, marking its second filing, and later sold its intellectual property to CJS Group. A'Gaci, a women's fashion brand, also filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in August, marking its second time in bankruptcy court in under two years. In 2019, several major retailers faced bankruptcy, including Avenue, Barneys New York, Fred's, and Forever 21. Avenue, a plus-size apparel brand, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in August and later transitioned to Chapter 7, beginning the liquidation of over 200 stores. Barneys New York, a high-end department store chain, also filed for Chapter 11 in August, with its brands and intellectual property sold to Authentic Brands. Fred's, a discount retailer and pharmacy chain, filed for Chapter 11 in September, planning to liquidate over 500 stores. Forever 21, an apparel retailer, filed for Chapter 11 in September, with over 800 stores worldwide, and planned to exit most international markets. These bankruptcies highlighted challenges in the retail industry, including competition from larger rivals and operational difficulties. In 2019, the retail industry faced significant challenges as several companies filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy. One notable case was Sugarfina, a luxury candy brand known for its unique gummy bear and chocolate flavors. Sugarfina filed for bankruptcy in September 2019, listing assets and liabilities of up to $50 million. Private-equity firm Bristol Luxury Group acquired its assets in November, vowing to keep some stores open. Sugarfina also operated smaller shops in some Nordstrom locations. Another major player was Destination Maternity, which filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October 2019. The company, which owned maternity brands like A Pea in the Pod and Motherhood Maternity, had over 400 stores at the time. Marquee Brands acquired its assets in early December, stating it was evaluating all aspects of the business, including its retail store network. The future of Destination Maternity's locations under new ownership remains uncertain. These bankruptcies highlight the struggles faced by the retail sector during this period.

summary: President Donald Trump's tweets about Amazon are unlikely to lead to regulatory action against the company, according to antitrust experts. William Kovacic, a professor at George Washington University, stated that regulatory agencies like the FTC and DOJ are unlikely to be influenced by political pressure. Trump's criticism of Amazon, including calling it a 'no-tax monopoly,' may not result in any significant regulatory changes. However, the government could still take action against Amazon if it is found to be engaging in anti-competitive practices, such as favoring its own products over third-party sellers. The Trump administration could also use antitrust laws to challenge Amazon's acquisitions, such as its purchase of Whole Foods. While Trump's threats may not lead to immediate regulatory action, the government could still take steps to address Amazon's market dominance. Trump's threats against Amazon are largely symbolic, with antitrust experts suggesting that a case against the company would require substantial evidence, which is unlikely to be influenced by Trump's actions. Kovacic emphasized that while being in the spotlight may make companies more cautious, bringing a case against Amazon is not a straightforward process. In the short term, Trump's best opportunity to challenge Amazon is through the Postal Service, as the current five-year contract between Amazon and USPS is set to expire in October. A report by Teddy Downey suggests that USPS sales officials may begin negotiations for a new deal as early as April 15, which could result in Amazon paying up to 41% more for its average package. Advisors are also pushing Trump to cancel Amazon's pending contract with the Department of Defense for cloud computing services. Additionally, Trump could target Amazon for its lenient policies on Chinese manufacturers, though he has not yet addressed this issue publicly.

summary: Copper prices surged to their highest level since November 2014, reaching $3.0015 per pound for September delivery futures. The rise in copper prices positively impacted shares of Freeport McMoRan and BHP Billiton, which rose 4.1 percent and 1.2 percent, respectively. Traders view copper as a bellwether for global economic performance due to its use in manufacturing, housing, and development. The Eurozone economy grew 2.5 percent in the second quarter, exceeding the European Commission's estimated potential growth of 1.7 percent for 2017. Japan's GDP also rose 4 percent, surpassing expectations. A weaker U.S. dollar, strong demand from China, and speculation about a potential Chinese ban on scrap metal imports have further boosted copper prices. Net income came in at $14.1 billion, or $2.91 per share. Apple repurchased $19.4 billion in shares, with cumulative repurchases reaching $239 billion. As the US debt grows, here are 23 debt-free companies. CNBC research shows that only about 23 companies in the S&P 500 have managed to stay debt-free. When looking at the year-to-date stock performance, only eight of these names are outperforming the S&P 500. These companies include Chipotle (CMG), MasterCard (MA), Bed Bath & Beyond (BBBY), Paychex (PAYX), Visa (V), Akamai (AKAM), Robert Half (RHI), and Forest Labs (FRX). Among these, Mastercard, Paychex, Visa, and Robert Half all pay a dividend. Lazard Capital's Managing Director Art Hogan notes that having no debt isn't necessarily a big plus for a company and that it is actually a favorable time for companies to take on debt. He adds that companies continue to have reasonable debt-to-equity ratios and that most of the selling pressure seen in this current uncertainty has been agnostic of debt levels. Debt-Free Companies include: Chipotle (CMG), MasterCard (MA), Bed Bath & Beyond (BBBY), Paychex (PAYX), Visa (V), Akamai (AKAM), Robert Half (RHI), Forest Labs (FRX), Garmin (GRMN), Cognizant Technology (CTSH), T. In contrast, sectors like Telecom, Utilities, and Consumer Staples have the highest debt-to-total assets ratios at 46 percent, 36 percent, and 34 percent, respectively. summary: On October 22, 2015, the U.S. Treasury postponed the 2-year note auction originally scheduled for October 27, 2015, due to debt ceiling constraints. The 5-year and 7-year note auctions on October 28 and 29, 2015, proceeded as planned, with settlements on November 2, 2015. Treasury estimated that extraordinary measures would be exhausted by November 3, 2015, leaving less than $30 billion to meet commitments. Postponing the 2-year note auction was deemed less risky for market functioning than delaying the 5-year or 7-year note. The debt limit impasse also increased borrowing costs, reduced Treasury bill supply, and raised operational risks. Treasury has reduced debt issuance and cash balances, falling below a $150 billion minimum level. The 13-week, 26-week, and 2-year floating rate auctions were also announced on October 22, 2015.

summary: The U.S. manufacturing sector experienced growth in February 2022, with the Manufacturing PMI® at 58.6%, up 1 percentage point from January's 57.6%. The New Orders Index rose to 61.7%, indicating strong demand, while the Production Index increased to 58.5%. However, the Employment Index dipped to 52.9%, reflecting ongoing challenges with staffing and turnover. Supplier Deliveries slowed at a faster rate, and the Prices Index rose to 75.6%, showing continued inflationary pressures. The Backlog of Orders Index hit 65%, signaling a surge in pending orders. The report highlights a demand-driven environment with supply chain constraints, as the omicron variant's impact waned, and recovery is expected in March. The six largest manufacturing industries showed moderate-to-strong growth, with new export orders and backlogs reaching historically high levels. The February 2022 Manufacturing PMI® was reported at 58.6, indicating continued growth. This marks a slight increase from the previous month's 57.6. The report highlights that 16 manufacturing industries experienced growth, including Apparel, Leather & Allied Products, Textile Mills, and Transportation Equipment. The only industry reporting a decrease was Wood Products. Respondents noted challenges such as supply chain issues, particularly with electronic components and ocean freight, and the ongoing impact of the microchip shortage on the automotive sector. The New Orders index rose to 61.7, showing strong demand. The report also mentions that prices are increasing at a slower rate, and there is a growing backlog of orders. Commodities such as Aluminum, Steel, and Semiconductors are in short supply, while others like High Density Polyethylene and Polypropylene are down in price. The Institute for Supply Management (ISM) released its February 2022 Manufacturing Report On Business, indicating a PMI® of 58.6%, reflecting continued expansion in the U.S. manufacturing sector. This marks a positive trend, as the PMI remains above the 50 threshold, which signifies growth. The report highlights the resilience of the manufacturing industry amid ongoing economic challenges. The data underscores the sector's ability to adapt and thrive, contributing to the broader economic landscape. The report is a key indicator for assessing the health of the manufacturing economy and is widely followed by investors and policymakers. Additionally, Walgreens plans to test grocery pickups at its locations through a partnership with Kroger. The company's co-chief operating officer, Alex Gourlay, emphasized the importance of strategic partnerships, stating that Walgreens believes in collaborations that either accelerate its own work or bring capabilities it cannot easily develop. title: FRB: FEDS Notes: Has the inflation risk premium fallen? Is it now negative?
summary: The Federal Reserve Board's FEDS Notes examine whether the inflation risk premium has fallen and may now be negative. Inflation compensation, defined as the extra yield investors require for holding nominal assets exposed to inflation risk compared to inflation-adjusted returns like TIPS, has declined significantly since August 2014. Market-based measures of inflation compensation, calculated as the difference between zero-coupon nominal and T,IPS yields, have remained below 2 percent, the long-term inflation target of the FOMC. The analysis suggests that a long-term decline in the inflation risk premium may explain a significant portion of the recent reduction in inflation compensation. The FEDS Notes highlight that the decline in far-forward inflation compensation may reflect a decrease in the inflation risk premium rather than a drop in expected inflation rates. The VIX, a measure of equity market risk premium, has increased slightly over the past year as betas have declined, indicating a more negative inflation risk premium.

events.quote: Since August 2014, measures of inflation compensation have trended down noticeably
According to these commentaries, long-term nominal interest rates have generally exceeded short-term nominal interest rates, on average, to a greater degree than is true for yields
The correlation trended up over time and switched signs recently, implying that the risk premium may now be negative.
Using a-back-of-the-envelope calculation, we can roughly gauge the plausible magnitude of the negative risk premium.

Netflix (NFLX) reported a loss of 200,000 subscribers during the first quarter of 2022, marking its first subscriber decline in over a decade. The company attributed this to increased competition, password sharing, inflation, and the ongoing Russian invasion of Ukraine. Netflix's shares dropped over 25% following the report, and other streaming stocks like Roku, Spotify, and Disney also fell. The company warned of further subscriber losses, forecasting a global paid subscriber loss of 2 million for the second quarter. Netflix also mentioned the suspension of its service in Russia and the winding down of Russian memberships, which contributed to the loss of 700,000 subscribers. The company estimates that over 100 million additional households share access to its service, raising concerns about a potential global crackdown on password sharing. Netflix reported Q1 2022 earnings, with revenue increasing nearly 10% to $7.87 billion, slightly below analyst expectations of $7.93 billion. Net income fell 6.4% to $1.6 billion, down from $1.7 billion the previous year. Excluding items, the company earned $3.53 per share, surpassing the $2.89 per share expected by analysts. Free cash flow rose to $802 million, up from $692 million a year earlier. The company increased content spending, particularly on originals, to gain market share, but raised prices, leading to a loss of 600,000 subscribers in the U.S. and Canada. Analysts are questioning what additional strategies Netflix can implement to boost profits beyond its current initiatives.

summary: The Federal Reserve Board approved a final policy statement outlining the framework for setting the Countercyclical Capital Buffer (CCyB). summary: The Federal Reserve Board's FEDS Notes, published on December 3, 2015, examine credit-to-GDP trends and gaps by lender and credit type. The credit-to-GDP gap is defined as the difference between the level of private nonfinancial sector credit-to-GDP and its one-sided Hodrick-Prescott (HP) filtered trend. This variable is a key component in the Basel III countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) framework proposed by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS). The BCBS guidance emphasizes the credit-to-GDP gap as a common reference point for national authorities in formulating and explaining CCyB decisions. The European Union's Capital Requirements Directive (CRD) IV requires each E.U. country to calculate and publish the gap quarterly. In the U.S., the final joint interagency rule implementing Basel III includes the credit-to-GDP ratio among variables that may inform CCyB decisions. The study focuses on the aggregate credit-to-GDP ratio and investigates underlying developments by disaggregating the numerator by lender type and credit type. The HP filtered trends and gaps for the disaggregated ratios sum exactly to those of the aggregate series. The Federal Reserve Board's FEDS Notes analyze credit-to-GDP trends and gaps by lender and credit type. Figure 1 highlights the private nonfinancial credit-to-GDP ratio, with IF.PF.MF denoting insurance companies, pension funds, and long-term mutual funds. Other nonbanks include finance companies, private label ABS issuers, mortgage REITS, funding corporations, and broker-dealers. The credit-to-GDP trend is disaggregated by lender type and credit type, showing that GSEs and other nonbanks account for most of the increase in the one-sided trend. The BCBS CCyB Guidance suggests that the trend component should be excluded from policy considerations as it approximates the sustainable level of credit. However, the significant growth in GSE portfolios during the financial crisis was driven by unsustainable leverage, indicating that the trend may not always reflect sustainability. Similarly, the rapid increase in other nonbank credit was underpinned by a vulnerable liability system. The HP filter, used to calculate the trend, gives higher weights to recent observations, allowing for quicker detection of structural breaks. This approach may be appropriate for economies experiencing financial deepening but less so for mature systems like the U.S., where persistent credit-to-GDP increases may signal underlying vulnerabilities.

summary: The U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) released data showing that retail trade, finance and insurance, and utilities were the leading contributors to the 2.1 percent increase in real GDP in the fourth quarter of 2019. Real value added for retail trade increased 7.4 percent, primarily due to an increase in other retail, including gasoline stations and nonstore retailers. Finance and insurance saw a 5.1 percent increase, with securities, commodity contracts, and investments being the largest contributors. Utilities increased 23.3 percent, mainly due to an increase in electric power generation. Nondurable goods manufacturing decreased 2.8 percent, reflecting declines in food and beverage, tobacco, and petroleum products. Other services, except government, decreased 1.6 percent, with repair and maintenance and personal services being the main contributors to the decline. Construction increased 1.4 percent, after a 2.1 percent decrease in the third quarter. Real gross output increased 1.1 percent in the fourth quarter, with the private services-producing sector contributing 1.7 percent, the private goods-producing sector decreasing 1.4 percent, and the government sector increasing 2.8 percent. Real GDP for the U.S. increased 2.3 percent in 2019, driven by growth in private goods- and services-producing sectors and the government sector. The U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) reported that in the fourth quarter and year 2019, real GDP growth was widespread, with 20 of 22 industry groups contributing to the increase. Professional, scientific, and technical services; finance and insurance; and information were the leading contributors to the increase in real GDP in 2019. For professional, scientific, and technical services, real value added increased 5.5 percent in 2019, after increasing 5.2 percent in 2018. The 2019 increase primarily reflected increases in miscellaneous professional, scientific, and technical services as well as computer systems design. Finance and insurance increased 3.3 percent in 2019, after decreasing 1.9 percent in 2018. The 2019 increase followed two consecutive years of decline and primarily reflected an increase in insurance carriers and related activities. Information services increased 4.6 percent in 2019, after increasing 8.5 percent in 2018. The 2019 increase primarily reflected increases in data processing, internet publishing, and other information services as well as publishing industries.

summary: The White House has warned that climate change could cost the U.S. federal budget about $2 trillion each year by the end of the century, with additional annual spending of $25 billion to $128 billion in areas such as coastal disaster relief, flood insurance, and crop insurance. The Office of Management and Budget (OMB) highlighted the fiscal risks of climate change, emphasizing that future damages could dwarf current damages if greenhouse gas emissions continue unabated. The report was released on April 4, 2022, the same day as the United Nations' climate science panel's report, which warned that global warming must be slashed to 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels, requiring greenhouse gas emissions to peak before 2025. The U.S. has already warmed about 1.1 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels and is on track to experience a global temperature rise of 2.4 degrees Celsius by 2100. Climate change could cost the U.S. up to $2 trillion annually by 2100, according to the White House. The analysis highlights rising costs from extreme weather events, including more frequent hurricanes that could increase annual spending on coastal disaster response to between $22 billion and $94 billion by 2100. Additionally, 12,000 federal buildings could be flooded by 10 feet due to rising sea levels, with replacement costs exceeding $43.7 billion. A 2021 report from the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration predicted sea level rise in the U.S. between 0.6 meters and 2.2 meters by the end of the century. President Joe Biden's 2023 budget proposal includes nearly $45 billion in new funding for climate change, clean energy, and environmental justice programs, representing a 60% increase over the 2021 fiscal year. The Build Back Better Act, a $1.75 trillion House-passed bill, would be the largest federal clean energy investment and could help the U.S. achieve about half of Biden's emissions reduction goal by 2030.

summary: KENTUCKY BANCSHARES, INC. (the Company) terminated its Retirement Plan and Trust (the Plan) in a standard termination on December 31, 2008. The termination was influenced by the Pension Protection Act of 2006 (PPA), which amended Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 417(e)(3) and changed the definition of applicable interest rate, leading to a decrease in the value of plan benefits. The Company amended the Plan on February 24, 2009, to comply with the PPA, and the Internal Revenue Service issued a favorable determination in July 2010. However, the Plan was later selected for audit by the PBGC, which claimed that the 2009 amendment violated PBGC Regulation Section 4041.8(a) by lowering benefits. The PBGC filed a complaint in May 2013 to require additional distributions to Plan beneficiaries. On March 17, 2014, the United States District Court (Eastern District of Kentucky) issued an Opinion and Order entering judgment in favor of the PBGC and ruling that the Company must comply with the PBGC's determination respecting the Plan. The Company is appraising its options with respect to this judgment, including an appeal of the decision. However, in light of the court's opinion, the Company has now accrued approximately $1.6 million as of December 31, 2013 for this matter. After taking into account income tax adjustments and indemnification undertakings from professionals who assisted the Company in the termination of the Plan, the impact is an approximate $470,000 decrease to the net income disclosed on Form 8-K filed by the Company on January 31, 2014. Moreover, in the event the subject court decision is not overturned, the Company believes it has claims for further contribution towards payment of this liability from professionals who assisted the Company in the termination of the Plan.

Sovereign wealth funds (SWFs) are increasingly investing in real estate amid volatile stock markets, according to an analyst. Michael Maduell, president of the Sovereign Wealth Fund Institute, noted that SWFs are seeking long-term investments where they can secure their capital without needing to reinvest frequently. The institute analyzes investments by public asset owners, including SWFs and other long-term governmental investors. Pension funds and endowments are also boosting their real estate and infrastructure investments. Norway's Government Pension Fund Global, the world's largest sovereign wealth fund with over $830 billion in assets under management (AUM), increased its real estate allocation and is exploring core property markets in Asia. Saudi Arabia unveiled a 15-year plan to transform its economy, with the country's sovereign wealth fund expected to grow from $200 billion in AUM to $6.5 trillion in March 2016. Preqin's research indicated that commodities funds have suffered due to the shift into real estate and other stable investments, with SWF holdings dropping 50% in March. Additionally, oil prices remaining low have led exporting countries to liquidate assets to fund government spending. Saudi Arabia also announced the listing of its state-owned oil company, Saudi Aramco, with plans to sell a stake valued at over $2 trillion, with proceeds going into a new sovereign wealth fund.

summary: Nike reported its fiscal fourth-quarter 2019 earnings, which slightly missed analysts' expectations. Revenues increased by 4% to just over $10 billion, driven by higher sales of sneakers and sports gear. However, the company's earnings per share of 62 cents fell short of the forecasted 66 cents. Nike's margins were impacted by its direct-to-consumer investments. The brand's revenue, excluding Converse, rose 10% to $9.7 billion, while Converse sales remained flat at $491 million. North America sales increased 8% to $4.17 billion, and China sales surged 22% to $1.70 billion. Nike has faced challenges in growing sales in the U.S. due to competition from brands like Adidas and Lululemon. Footwear sales in North America rose 9%, while apparel and equipment sales grew by 6% and 7%, respectively. Nike's direct-to-consumer division generated $11.8 billion in revenue, fueled by a 35% increase in online sales. The company also emphasized its efforts to expand its women's business and improve customer engagement through initiatives like the Nike Fit app. Nike reported its fiscal fourth-quarter 2019 earnings, highlighting its continued focus on expanding its women's business and leveraging digital opportunities. The company noted that its direct-to-consumer women's business is still outperforming the wholesale channel. Despite ongoing trade tensions between the U.S. and China, Nike emphasized its strong presence in the Chinese market, stating that consumer sentiment remains positive. Nike's stock closed up over 1% on Thursday, with a year-to-date increase of 17%, contributing to a market cap of approximately $131.4 billion. The stock has significantly outperformed the S&P 500 Retail ETF (XRT), which has declined by 14% over the same period.

The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has charged Scott London, a former KPMG partner, and his friend Bryan Shaw with insider trading. London, who was in charge of KPMG's Pacific Southwest audit practice, allegedly provided Shaw with confidential information about five KPMG audit clients, enabling Shaw to make over $1.2 million in illicit profits. The two men met at a country club and became close friends and golfing partners. London allegedly provided the information to help Shaw overcome financial struggles after his family-run jewelry business faltered. In exchange, Shaw paid London at least $50,000 in cash and gave him an expensive Rolex watch and other gifts. The SEC alleges that London began providing Shaw with nonpublic information in October 2010 and continued for 18 months. Shaw traded on this information, making over $714,000 from trading on confidential data about Herbalife, Skechers, and Deckers. London also gained access to information about mergers involving RSC Holdings and Pacific Capital, allowing Shaw to profit from these transactions. The SEC's complaint charges London and Shaw with violations of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5. The SEC seeks to order them to disgorge ill-gotten gains, pay interest, and face financial penalties. summary: The Federal Reserve issued Supervisory Letter SR 12-17 / CA 12-14 on December 17, 2012, outlining a consolidated supervision framework for large financial institutions. This framework was revised on October 1, 2025, to remove references to reputational risk. The letter emphasizes enhancing the resiliency of financial institutions to withstand internal and external stresses, ensuring they maintain sufficient capital, liquidity, and operational resilience. It also aims to reduce the impact on the financial system and broader economy in the event of a firm’s failure or material weakness. The framework incorporates both microprudential and macroprudential considerations, aligning with provisions of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act. The guidance does not apply to community banking organizations, defined as institutions with total consolidated assets of $10 billion or less. The framework outlines a tailored supervisory approach for large financial institutions, focusing on systemic risk and firm-specific vulnerabilities. It applies to LISCC firms, which are the largest and most complex U.S. and foreign financial organizations subject to consolidated supervision. Nonbank financial companies designated by the FSOC are also included. Large Banking Organizations (LBOs) and Large Foreign Banking Organizations (Large FBOs) are defined based on their consolidated assets. The framework emphasizes enhancing resiliency through capital and liquidity planning, corporate governance, recovery planning, and resolution strategies. The Federal Reserve may identify additional priorities beyond these core areas to improve supervision and address risks to financial stability. Effective supervision requires cooperation with other regulators and a comprehensive understanding of each firm's condition.

Foreign carmakers are increasingly targeting the U.S. sedan market as Detroit automakers shift focus toward SUVs and crossovers. Over the past decade, sedans, coupes, and other passenger cars accounted for more than half of the new vehicle market, but by the end of November 2018, that share had dropped to 30.5 percent. This decline is expected to continue for several more years. As the Detroit Big Three scale back sedan production, foreign competitors like Honda, Nissan, Toyota, and Audi are capitalizing on the opportunity. General Motors announced it would discontinue six popular sedans, while Ford had already planned to phase out most passenger cars, except for the Mustang. Fiat Chrysler has also moved in the same direction. However, some analysts question whether the Big Three are overreacting, as foreign automakers are also expanding their utility vehicle lines. For example, Hyundai, which saw a sharp decline in sales, has added three new utility vehicles, including the Palisade, the largest SUV it has ever offered. Meanwhile, Mercedes-Benz USA remains bullish on sedans, despite the industry trend. The Los Angeles Auto Show highlighted the shift, with many new SUVs and crossovers debuting, but also some new passenger cars like the updated Nissan Maxima and the redesigned Mazda3. Honda has maintained its presence in the sedan segment with models like the Accord and Civic, which are expected to sell at least 700,000 units in the U.S. this year. The company also introduced the new Insight hybrid, which was recognized as a finalist for the North American Car of the Year and the Green Car of the Year. Similarly, Toyota is reevaluating its sedan lineup, with CEO Jim Lentz acknowledging the need to focus on profitable segments. While overall light truck demand has kept auto sales from declining significantly, compact and midsize sedans have seen sharp declines, with Honda and Toyota experiencing drops of 12.6% and 17.3%, respectively. Despite these challenges, foreign automakers like Honda and Toyota continue to emphasize their commitment to sedans, highlighting the ongoing competition in the U.S. market.

The probe followed a Bloomberg article that revealed the company had secretly bought back Just Mayo from grocery stores. Hampton Creek denied any wrongdoing, and its founder, Josh Tetrick, stated the company would share the facts rather than the inaccuracies reported by Bloomberg. The company had raised nearly $220 million in venture capital, including investments from billionaires like Marc Benioff and Vinod Khosla. summary: Gold prices fell on Tuesday as the U.S. dollar strengthened, with investors anticipating the Federal Reserve may soon end or taper its economic stimulus program. Spot gold extended losses to 0.81 percent at $1,242.81, after rising earlier to a near one-week high at $1,267.20 an ounce. U.S. gold futures for August delivery lost 1.09 percent to $1,242 an ounce. The dollar rose to a five-week peak against a basket of currencies on a broad view that the Federal Reserve will scale back its stimulus measures sooner than expected given the recent run of generally solid U.S. economic data. Investors are looking ahead to Friday's U.S. labor report, with expectations of 165,000 new jobs in June and a lower unemployment rate of 7.5 percent. Some analysts warned that gold's recovery from last week's three-year low at $1,180.70 was not likely to last for long, with some participants anticipating eventual price declines to $1,000 an ounce. Gold prices settled lower as the US dollar strengthened, with SPDR Gold Trust, the world's largest gold exchange-traded fund, reporting an outflow of 1.2 tonnes to 968.30 tonnes on Monday, its lowest since February 2009. Holdings have dropped 382.5 tonnes since the start of the year. Physical demand has not rescued gold as it did in April, when prices fell the most in 30 years. However, Shanghai futures were trading at more than a $30 premium to spot prices, indicating some renewed interest. Commodity market brokers Marex Spectron noted that there "has been some good physical demand with premiums in Asia remaining elevated ... (showing) that buyers believe that gold has probably done enough on the downside for now." In Hong Kong and Singapore, gold bar premiums remained at the same levels as last week, indicating demand had not picked up strongly. Silver was down with gold, losing 1.38 percent to $19.29 an ounce, reaching a near three-year low at $18.19 on Friday. Platinum fell 0.89 percent to $1,362.24 an ounce and palladium dropped 0.44 percent to $681.47 an ounce.

summary: Fidel Castro's biggest financial regrets reveal his acknowledgment of past decisions that impacted Cuba's economic stability. During a meeting with Bill Rhodes, a former Citigroup executive, Castro admitted regret over expelling the International Monetary Fund (IMF) from Cuba during the early days of the communist revolution. He believed that staying a member of the IMF, along with the World Bank and the Inter-American Development Bank, could have provided crucial support for Cuba's economic challenges. Additionally, Castro expressed regret over placing Ernesto 'Che' Guevara in charge of the Cuban central bank, acknowledging that Guevara lacked financial expertise. Guevara, known for his role in the Cuban Revolution and his brutal tactics against political enemies, later led the seizure of American banks in Cuba, including branches of Citigroup, Bank of America, and JPMorgan Chase. These actions contributed to Cuba's debt issues, with an estimated $5 billion still outstanding from the mid-1980s. Fidel Castro has expressed significant financial regrets, particularly regarding the nationalization of Cuban assets and the impact of the U.S. trade embargo. In a conversation with former U.S. Ambassador to Cuba, Peter Rhodes, Castro stated that he did not believe Cuba owed Citigroup any money for the seized banks, as Citigroup had frozen Cuban assets held in New York. This sentiment was further elaborated in an essay published in a Communist Party newspaper following the reopening of the U.S. embassy in Cuba after 54 years. Castro argued that the United States owes Cuba "many millions of dollars" in damages from the trade embargo, which lasted for half a century. He also criticized the U.S. for removing the dollar from the gold standard in 1971. Rhodes, who had previously disagreed with Castro's stance on debts to Citigroup, noted that the government of Cuba owed them on loans that could not be collected due to nationalization. Reflecting on the conversation, Rhodes called it "a fascinating conversation."

summary: Kraft Heinz shares fell more than 13% on Thursday, hitting an all-time low, as the packaged food giant delayed its quarterly filing and disclosed write-downs totaling $1.22 billion. The company had previously received a subpoena from the Securities and Exchange Commission into its accounting policies and internal controls. The SEC investigation led to an internal review, causing Kraft Heinz to delay its annual report filing twice. In May, Warren Buffett, one of the company's largest investors, mentioned that Kraft Heinz was in "a dispute with its auditor." The internal review identified adjustments that resulted in an understatement of the cost of products sold totaling $208 million, including misstatements of $175 million. Kraft Heinz then cautioned that the SEC investigation was ongoing. The company also delayed filing its quarterly reports for the first and second quarters of 2019 due to a "material weakness" in its cash flow projections allocation to certain brands. Kraft Heinz experienced a significant drop in its stock price following the release of its earnings report. The company reported a decline in net income for the first half of the year, with earnings dropping to half of what they were in the same period in 2018. Additionally, Kraft Heinz recorded a $744 million write-down for its Eastern emerging markets, Brazilian, U.S. refrigerated, and Latin America exports businesses. The company also wrote down its Miracle Whip, Velveeta, Lunchables, Maxwell House, Philadelphia, and Cool Whip brands by $474 million. Despite exploring options for its Maxwell House brand, including a potential sale, the company has faced limited interest. Kraft Heinz also pulled the sale of several other brands and delayed the potential sale of its Ore-Ida frozen potato business. For the second quarter ended June 29, the company earned $449 million, or 37 cents per share, down from $754 million, or 62 cents per share, a year earlier. Excluding impairment charges, earnings were 78 cents per share, which was better than the 75 cents per share analysts had expected. Revenue fell to $6.41 billion, from $6.69 billion a year ago, and sales were below estimates of $6.58 billion. The company did not provide an outlook for this year's financial targets.

title: Federal Reserve Board - Federal Reserve issues FOMC statement
summary: On June 20, 2012, the Federal Reserve issued its FOMC statement. Economic expansion remained moderate, but employment growth had slowed. Unemployment remained high. Business investment continued to rise, while household spending growth decelerated. The housing sector remained weak. Inflation declined due to lower oil and gas prices, with long-term inflation expectations stable. The Fed aimed to achieve maximum employment and price stability. The Fed also announced that economic growth would remain moderate and gradually improve, with the unemployment rate expected to decline slowly. Global financial strains posed significant risks. Inflation was anticipated to stay at or below the rate consistent with its dual mandate. The Fed would maintain a highly accommodative monetary policy, keeping the federal funds rate at 0 to 1/4 percent through late 2014. The Fed would continue its securities maturity extension program, purchasing long-term Treasury securities and redeeming short-term ones to lower longer-term interest rates and ease financial conditions. The FOMC voted to take further action to promote a stronger economic recovery and sustained improvement in labor market conditions while maintaining price stability. Jeffrey M. summary: Climate change litigation is becoming a powerful tool in the global fight against environmental degradation. From California to the Philippines, activists, governments, and citizens are increasingly turning to the courts to hold polluters and national governments accountable for the effects of climate change. The number of climate-related lawsuits has surged over the past few decades, with the U.S. and non-U.S. jurisdictions both seeing a significant rise in cases. In the U.S., many recent lawsuits involve plaintiffs seeking to protect climate rules established under former President Barack Obama, while in Europe, governments are being challenged over insufficient pollution-reduction plans. Julia Olson, an attorney for Our Children’s Trust, emphasized that courts are now the last hope for preventing irreversible harm to the planet. California has become a focal point for climate litigation, with eight cities and counties suing oil companies to recover costs related to rising sea levels. Cases in San Francisco and Oakland face dismissal motions, with major oil companies like Chevron, BP, ExxonMobil, ConocoPhilips, and Royal Dutch Shell arguing that climate remedies should be handled by lawmakers, not judges. BP’s CEO, Bob Dudley, acknowledged the risk of legal action during the company’s annual meeting, highlighting the growing influence of climate litigation as a business concern. While many cases aim to push governments and companies toward greater climate action, some are also used to oppose environmental protections, as seen in ExxonMobil’s dispute with Massachusetts and New York. Climate change litigation is becoming a powerful tool for cities and governments to hold fossil fuel companies accountable. In the U.S., New York City has sued five major oil companies, arguing they are financially liable for climate change damages. The Trump administration and 15 states support the companies, claiming that court orders could force the government to revise its energy policies. The U.S. Justice Department argues that such lawsuits empower individuals globally to file similar claims. Similar cases are expected in the Netherlands and France. Human rights arguments are also being used, with cases like those in the Philippines and Switzerland highlighting how climate change threatens basic rights. In Germany, environmental groups have successfully pushed for diesel car bans, and the European Commission is taking several countries to court over air pollution. These legal actions reflect a broader power struggle between governments and environmental advocates.

title: Speech by Chairman Bernanke on some reflections on the crisis and the policy response - Federal Reserve Board
summary: During the 2008 financial crisis, Bernanke emphasized the distinction between triggers and vulnerabilities. Triggers included subprime mortgage market developments, while vulnerabilities encompassed systemic weaknesses such as high leverage, unstable funding, and inadequate risk management. Paper losses from housing price swings were significantly greater than subprime losses, with a 30% decline eliminating $7 trillion in wealth. Bernanke noted that housing price declines, while significant, may not fully explain the crisis's severity, as much of the drop occurred after the crisis peak. The interaction between housing, mortgage, and financial system weaknesses amplified the crisis. Shadow banking, operating outside traditional regulation, contributed to systemic risks through securitization vehicles, ABCP conduits, money market mutual funds, and repos. It facilitated maturity transformation and channeled savings into debt-like instruments. Rapid growth was driven by regulatory arbitrage and demand for cash-like assets. Commercial banks faced limitations due to restrictions on interest on business checking accounts and FDIC-insured deposit limits. A key vulnerability was reliance on short-term wholesale funding, including commercial paper and interbank loans.

title: Federal Reserve Board - Federal Reserve Board approves final rule to help ensure banks maintain strong capital positions
summary: The Federal Reserve Board approved a final rule to ensure banks maintain strong capital positions, enabling them to continue lending during economic downturns. The rule addresses capital requirements for larger banks and implements Basel III reforms and Dodd-Frank Act changes. It mandates higher quality and quantity of capital, including a minimum common equity tier 1 capital ratio of 4.5% and a 2.5% conservation buffer. The rule also raises the minimum tier 1 capital to risk-weighted assets ratio from 4% to 6%, introduces a 4% minimum leverage ratio for all banking organizations, and adds a new supplementary leverage ratio for large, internationally active banks to account for off-balance sheet exposures. Chairman Ben Bernanke emphasized that these changes will improve resilience during financial stress, supporting the U.S. economy.

Best Buy is testing new store formats, including smaller sales floors and experiential locations, as it adapts to changing consumer behavior post-pandemic. summary: Facebook's stock dropped 4.5% on Friday following CEO Mark Zuckerberg's announcement that the newsfeed will continue to favor content from people over publishers, even if it may reduce engagement metrics. Despite the stock decline, Wall Street analysts had mixed but generally positive reactions. Some analysts, like Samuel Kemp from Piper Jaffray, viewed the change as a long-term positive for the platform, arguing that it could help combat user attrition and that Facebook's ownership of Instagram could absorb any lost ad revenue. Brian Nowak from Morgan Stanley, however, urged caution, noting the uncertainty surrounding the changes. Overall, the market reaction was lukewarm, with analysts raising price targets for the company's next earnings report. Facebook's stock faced downward pressure following news of a potential Newsfeed change, with Wall Street analysts offering mixed reactions. Brian Wieser of Pivotal Research Group expressed concerns that the company's actions could pose a headwind to growth in the short term, though he acknowledged long-term benefits. Wieser noted that Facebook's user usage was already declining before the announcement, and he suggested that the company's efforts to address fake news could help. Justin Post from BofA Merrill Lynch emphasized the importance of engagement metrics, noting that Facebook has not disclosed average daily time spent. Scott Kessler of CFRA Research highlighted the short-term revenue impact but praised the move for brand value. Daniel Ives of GBH Insights remained optimistic, citing Facebook's strong monetization potential and its global user base. Ives raised his price target for Facebook to $225, a nearly 20% increase from the previous close.

title: The market for semiconductor lithography equipment is expected to grow at a CAGR of 10.2 % over the forecast period (2021 - 2026)
summary: The semiconductor lithography equipment market is projected to grow at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 10.2% from 2021 to 2026. Lithography machines are essential in chip manufacturing, enabling the printing of minute circuits on semiconductors, which support information-oriented societies. These systems are crucial for producing semiconductor devices used in cameras, smartphones, and automobiles. The evolution of lithography technology includes g-line, i-line, and excimer laser (KrF/ArF) steppers. EUVL, a next-generation lithography technology, is being developed for ultra-fine exposure. Critical Dimension Process Control equipment is also in high demand. Companies like Imec and ASML are collaborating to advance EUV lithography for high-volume production. The outbreak of the novel coronavirus is expected to negatively impact silicon wafer sales in the second half of 2020, potentially affecting price negotiations in 2021. Consumer electronics sales are forecast to decline due to shifting consumer preferences, which may reduce the usage of semiconductor lithography equipment.

summary: The House passed the $1.9 trillion American Rescue Plan, aimed at delivering financial relief to struggling families and ramping up vaccination distribution. The bill includes funding for vaccine production and distribution, another round of stimulus payments for many households, an extension of federal unemployment benefits, and more. The plan also introduces a fully refundable child tax credit for 2021, increasing the amount from $2,000 to $3,000 per child ages 6 to 17 and to $3,600 for children under the age of 6. The bill includes $30 billion in emergency rental assistance and an additional $5 billion to prevent Covid-19 outbreaks among homeless populations. It also earmarks $10 billion for mortgage assistance. The minimum wage increase to $15 per hour by 2025 was one of the most controversial provisions in the drafting of the bill. The House's $1.9 trillion American Rescue Plan includes provisions for a third economic impact payment, worth up to $1,400 per individual and dependent. The payments phase out gradually, hitting $0 for individuals earning an AGI over $100,000 per year and couples earning over $200,000 per year. The bill also extends key unemployment programs past their current March 14 expiration date through August 29, boosting enhanced federal payments from an extra $300 per week to $400. Additionally, the bill allocates $20 billion to create a national Covid-19 vaccination program and an additional $50 billion for virus testing. The American Rescue Plan also provides funding for schools, restaurants and bars, state and local aid, vaccine production and distribution, and paid leave. The Senate will likely pass a different version of the bill, and Democrats hope to have Biden sign the legislation by March 14.

summary: As the real estate market began to recover in May, home searches in suburban zip codes jumped 13%, according to realtor.com, one of the largest real estate listing websites. That doubled the pace of growth in urban areas. More than half of the nation's 100 largest metropolitan areas are seeing increased interest in the suburbs. Millennials, who once fueled downtown renewal and growth, are now piling out. The stay-at-home orders brought on by the coronavirus have more potential homebuyers looking for properties in the suburbs. Millennials are now the largest cohort of buyers. While homes are spending more time on the market overall, due to complications surrounding closings, both suburban and rural markets are not experiencing that lag time as much, due to very strong demand. Javier Vivas, realtor.com director of economic research, said, "This migration to the suburbs is not a new trend, but it has become more pronounced this spring. After several months of shelter-in-place orders, the desire to have more space and the potential for more people to work remotely are likely two of the factors contributing to the popularity of the burbs." Real estate agents in the New York City area have reported strong demand in the surrounding suburbs, as contracts on Manhattan apartments plunged 80% annually in May, according to Jonathan Miller of real estate appraisal firm Miller Samuel. This new flight to the suburbs is clearly benefiting the nation's homebuilders, who have seen a much quicker recovery than they ever expected. Stuart Miller, chairman and former CEO of Miami-based Lennar, said, "There's no question that there are people who are fleeing the cities. There's no question that the second home has been a place of refuge. There's no question people are rethinking whether they want to be in high rise rentals with common spaces as amenities vs. having a home of their own with a backyard."

summary: Toshiba Corp agreed to sell its chip division for 2 trillion yen ($17.7 billion) to a Bain Capital-led consortium. The consortium includes Apple, Dell Technologies Capital, and SK Hynix. title: Federal Reserve Board - Federal Reserve issues FOMC statement
summary: On July 29, 2015, the Federal Reserve issued a FOMC statement indicating that economic activity had been expanding moderately. Household spending growth remained moderate, while the housing sector showed additional improvement. Business fixed investment and net exports remained soft, but the labor market continued to improve with solid job gains and declining unemployment. Inflation remained below the Committee's longer-run objective, partly due to earlier energy price declines and decreasing non-energy import prices. The Committee emphasized its commitment to fostering maximum employment and price stability, expecting economic activity to expand at a moderate pace with labor market indicators moving toward levels consistent with its dual mandate. The Committee views risks to the outlook as nearly balanced, with inflation anticipated to remain near its recent low level in the near term but expected to rise gradually toward 2 percent over the medium term as the labor market improves and transitory effects of earlier energy and import price declines dissipate. The Committee reaffirmed its view that the current 0 to 1/4 percent target range for the federal funds rate remains appropriate.

summary: On February 4, 2016, the European Commission approved Western Digital Corporation's pending acquisition of SanDisk Corporation under the EU Merger Regulation. This approval satisfies one of the conditions for the closing of the acquisition, which remains subject to other customary closing conditions, including shareholder approvals and regulatory approvals. The approval is a significant step in the merger process, which is expected to bring benefits to both companies. The document also includes forward-looking statements regarding the anticipated benefits of the merger and the expected closing date with Western Digital's subsidiary, Schrader Acquisition Corporation. This 8-K filing from SanDisk Corp dated February 4, 2016, outlines the risks and uncertainties associated with the proposed merger between SanDisk Corp and Western Digital. The document highlights various factors that could affect the merger, including the inability to obtain stockholder approval, regulatory hurdles, integration challenges, and potential adverse impacts on business relationships. The risks are further detailed in the preliminary joint proxy statement/prospectus filed with the SEC on December 11, 2015, and amended on January 27, 2016. The filing also notes that forward-looking statements are subject to change and that actual results may differ materially from those expressed. The document serves as a disclosure of potential risks rather than an offer to sell or solicit an offer to buy.

FirstEnergy's stock surged over 12% on Monday following a $2.5 billion investment from Elliott Management, Bluescape Energy Partners, GIC, and Zimmer Partners. The investment aims to help the utility pay down $1.45 billion in debt and cover $750 million in pension obligations. The deal includes forming a working group to transition FirstEnergy into a regulated utility focused on transmission and distribution, which guarantees a stable rate of return. The investment comes as FirstEnergy seeks to exit its competitive power generation business, which has faced challenges due to falling natural gas prices, renewable energy growth, and weak power prices. The transformation plan also involves restructuring FirstEnergy's business, with Charles John Wilder, known for his work with TXU Corporation, playing a key role. The company plans to address its unwanted assets through potential bankruptcy, restructuring, or sale of FirstEnergy Solutions, its power generation subsidiary.

summary: This article evaluates the accuracy of the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) employment, labor force, and macroeconomic projections up to 2010. It highlights that while BLS generally steered customers toward the correct industry sectors, the magnitude of the decline in manufacturing was underestimated. The article also notes that the BLS projections for nonfarm payroll employment, manufacturing employment, labor force, GDP, and unemployment rate were compared with those of other government agencies such as the Congressional Budget Office (CBO), the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), and the Energy Information Administration (EIA). The mean absolute errors for BLS projections were found to be nearly equivalent to those of other agencies, with the exception of the 2010 unemployment rate projection, where BLS assumed a rate of 4.0 percent, while other agencies expected between 4.5 percent and 5.2 percent. The article also discusses the impact of the housing bubble and bust on construction employment and the unexpected rise in oil prices due to increased global demand and the commercial viability of fracking. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) evaluated its employment, labor force, and macroeconomic projections up to 2010. The analysis indicated that the unemployment rate of 4.0 percent was likely below the Non-Accelerating Inflation Rate of Unemployment (NAIRU), suggesting it was not sustainable. Starting from the 2002–12 projections, BLS adopted a 'full employment' assumption, aligning the unemployment rate with or near NAIRU. While the 2010 projections were optimistic, BLS's errors were comparable to other agencies in 2006 and 2008. The BLS projected a slightly higher margin of error in GDP growth to 2010 due to the low unemployment rate assumption. However, BLS performed best among agencies for GDP growth projections to 2006 and 2008. The mean absolute error in GDP growth projections was nearly equivalent to other agencies. Errors in the labor force growth projections were minimal, averaging 0.1 percent, similar to those of the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) and the Energy Information Administration (EIA). Most errors stemmed from the 2010 projections due to a rapid decline in the participation rate between 2008 and 2010. The BLS employment outlook was more optimistic than that of EIA, though neither anticipated the extent of recent manufacturing declines. EIA correctly projected manufacturing employment declines for all three 10-year intervals, while BLS projected slight increases. The mean absolute error for EIA's nonfarm payroll employment projections was smaller than BLS's. BLS consistently expected faster employment growth and lower unemployment rates than EIA. A naïve model, which assumes past growth rates will persist, was used as a benchmark. BLS projections outperformed the naïve model in at least half the variables, with a p-value significant at the 5-percent level. The BLS projections process begins with population size and composition forecasts, using U.S. Census Bureau data for 136 categories, including age, race, gender, and ethnic origin. These are then converted to civilian noninstitutional population (CNIP) projections, which include all persons 16 years and older not in penal or mental institutions.

Andreessen Horowitz, a prominent venture capital firm based in Menlo Park, has made a historic philanthropic pledge. All six partners at the firm have committed to donating at least half of their lifetime income from venture capital investments to charity. This marks the first time an entire VC firm has made such a pledge. Founding Partner Marc Andreessen hopes this will set an example for other private equity and venture capital funds. His partner, Ben Horowitz, noted that if the firm meets its goals of being a top-tier VC firm, this could mean billions of dollars for charity. The firm has backed over 100 companies, including Facebook, Groupon, Twitter, Zynga, Foursquare, and Instagram. It has raised a total of $2.7 billion since 2009 and has already returned the principal of its first $200 million fund to investors after just three years. The decision was influenced by the firm's culture, with partner Scott Weiss suggesting the idea during his interview for the role.

Department stores have lost their dominant position in the beauty industry as specialty retailers like Ulta Beauty and Sephora have gained traction. The global cosmetics industry is projected to reach $430 billion by 2022, driven by the rise of social media and influencer marketing. Influencers have become key players, with brands spending between $100 and thousands of dollars for a single post. Ulta Beauty, in particular, has thrived, with its stock rising over 1,250% since 2009 and a market cap of $14.4 billion. The company has expanded its physical presence, opening 67 new stores in the first 10 months of the year. Meanwhile, traditional department stores have struggled to compete with the specialized, experiential approach of modern beauty retailers. Department stores have lost their clout in the beauty industry, as specialty retailers like Ulta and Sephora have gained traction. Ulta's appeal has been bolstered by celebrity brands such as Kylie Cosmetics and its relationship with YouTube star James Charles. However, a pullback in the key color cosmetics category has affected Ulta's stock. Sephora, owned by LVMH, has adapted to shifting consumer trends by launching initiatives like Clean at Sephora, which focuses on ingredient transparency. The beauty industry has seen a rise in self-care products, with skin-care sales increasing by 48% over the past decade. Consumers are now prioritizing health and wellness, favoring natural and organic ingredients. Specialty retailers are also leveraging technology, such as Google's ad technology, to drive in-store sales. While department stores are struggling, specialty retailers are adapting to meet evolving consumer preferences.

summary: On July 18, 2012, the Financial Stability Oversight Council (FSOC) designated eight financial market utilities (FMUs) as systemically important under Title VIII of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act. These FMUs include entities such as The Clearing House Payments Company, L.L.C., CLS Bank International, Chicago Mercantile Exchange, Inc., and The Depository Trust Company. The designation subjects these firms to heightened risk management standards. The FSOC considered four factors when determining systemic importance: the aggregate monetary value of transactions processed, exposure to counterparties, interdependencies with other FMUs, and the effect of failure on critical markets. The Council’s decision followed a process that included notifying FMUs of proposed designations and allowing them 30 days to request a hearing, which none did. This action marks a key step in creating a safer financial system under Wall Street Reform. The Council also approved its 2012 Annual Report, which outlines its activities and findings on financial market issues.

summary: The article discusses the perception of the U.S. stock market during the summer of 2013 as one of the most hated bull markets ever. Despite a 15% gain in the S&P 500 by early July, the rally was fueled by low-quality stocks with low price-to-earnings ratios, zero dividend yields, high short interest, and weak analyst ratings. Jeffrey D. Saut from Raymond James warned of a potential meaningful decline, citing the market's reliance on extreme monetary easing and the lack of confidence in the recovery. Bespoke Investment Group highlighted that the smallest stocks and those with the lowest P/E ratios outperformed, while high-dividend stocks lagged. Jim Paulsen from Wells Capital Management noted that the rally reflected a shift in confidence, with investors moving away from low-beta, high-dividend stocks toward higher-risk, higher-reward assets. The article suggests that the market's recovery was driven by a renewed sense of sustainability and confidence, even though it was marked by volatility and uncertainty.

An internal audit by Ernst & Young found the Defense Logistics Agency (DLA) failed to properly track over $800 million in construction projects, Politico reported. The audit identified deficiencies in documentation for millions of dollars in property and equipment. DLA concurred with the findings, acknowledging a lack of complete documentation for military construction and real property. The audit also revealed at least $465 million in misstatements for construction projects, including those financed for the Army Corps of Engineers or other defense agencies. Insufficient documentation was found for around $384 million in spending for "in progress" projects. The Pentagon estimates its department-wide audit would cost $367 million in 2018 and another $551 million to fix problems. About 1,200 auditors are participating in the process. The audit also disclosed the Army had 39 Black Hawk helicopters not properly recorded in its system, and the Air Force identified hundreds of structures not in its real property system.
